body: Which of the computer networks will you recommend on a **University campus**?

options.hint: Correct. A **Campus Area Network** links the LANs of buildings on one campus.
A LAN covers one building or office, not a whole campus.
A MAN covers a city or town, e.g. Cape Coast and its environs.
A WAN spans countries or continents; the Internet is the largest WAN.

hint: Match the network to the size of the area it covers.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Networks are classified by **geographic span**: LAN (one building) → **CAN** (several buildings of one campus or institution, joined by a high-speed backbone) → MAN (a city) → WAN (regions, countries, the globe). A university campus is exactly the CAN case.

## Simplified explanation

Think of size: room/building = LAN, **campus = CAN**, city = MAN, world = WAN.

> [!tip]
> Memory hook: **L**ocal < **C**ampus < **M**etropolitan < **W**ide.

body: _______ is the language that computers use to communicate over the Internet.

options.hint: Broadband is a type of fast connection, not a language.
Dial-up is a slow connection through a phone line.
Correct. Protocols (TCP/IP) are the agreed rules or 'language' of the Internet.
Software runs on computers; it is not the shared communication language.

hint: What set of rules lets different networks talk without conflict?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

An **Internet protocol** is the set of rules that lets different computer networks exchange data without conflict. The standard suite is `TCP/IP`: **TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) breaks data into packets and reassembles them; **IP** (Internet Protocol) addresses and routes each packet.

## Simplified explanation

Computers from different makers can only 'talk' if they follow the same rules. Those rules are the **Internet protocol** (TCP/IP).

body: Which device is needed to enable the **digital** device and the **analogue** device communicate in order to transmit data?

options.hint: The computer produces digital signals; it needs another device to convert them.
Correct. A modem MOdulates digital signals into analogue and DEModulates them back.
A network is the connection of computers, not the converting device.
Software cannot convert electrical signals on a phone line.

hint: Its name comes from MOdulator–DEModulator.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **modem** (modulator–demodulator) converts the computer's **digital** signal into an **analogue** signal that can travel over telephone lines (dial-up), and converts incoming analogue signals back to digital. The UCC notes describe exactly this in the dial-up connection, which does not exceed `56 kbps`.

## Simplified explanation

The computer speaks digital, the phone line speaks analogue. The **modem** is the translator in between.

body: One needs to subscribe to a bigger _______ to enable a greater volume of information be transmitted at a time.

options.hint: Correct. Bandwidth is the speed and amount of data transferred, measured in bits per second.
A bigger computer does not increase what your connection can carry.
Memory stores data inside the computer; it does not carry data over the Internet.
Storage keeps data; it does not move data across the network.

hint: It is measured in bits per second (bps).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Bandwidth** is the speed and amount of information transferred from one place to another on the Internet, measured in **bits per second** (`bps`, `kbps`, `Mbps`). The bigger the bandwidth, the greater the volume transmitted at a time and the faster information moves.

## Simplified explanation

Bandwidth is like the width of a road: a wider road lets more cars (data) pass at once.

body: What is the most popular use of the Internet?

options.hint: E-commerce is a major use, but not the most popular one.
Correct. Email, chat, social media and video calls make communication the leading use.
Entertainment is popular but comes after communication.
Research is important for students, but it is not the most common use overall.

hint: Think of email, WhatsApp and social media.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The UCC notes list the uses of the Internet as **communication**, information dissemination, education and research, entertainment, online services and e-commerce, with **communication** (email, instant messaging, social networking, audio and video conferencing) as the most widespread.

## Simplified explanation

Most people go online to **talk to others**: email, chats and calls. That is communication.

body: Uniform Resource Locator (URL) is basically an Internet _______.

options.hint: Correct. A URL is the unique address of a resource on the Web.
A URL identifies where a resource is, but 'address' is the accepted term.
A hyperlink points to a URL; the URL itself is the address.
The URL locates a resource; it is not the resource itself.

hint: Like a house address, but for a web page.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **URL** (`Uniform Resource Locator`) is the address of a resource on the Web, e.g. `https://ucc.edu.gh/library`. It shows the **protocol** (`https`), the **domain** (`ucc.edu.gh`) and the **path** (`/library`). The domain ending (`.edu`, `.gov`, `.org`, `.com`) is also used when judging a source's **reliability**.

## Simplified explanation

A URL is the **web address** you type to reach a page.

body: The Internet has a centralized monitor where information that is put there is monitored.

options.hint: No single body monitors or controls everything published on the Internet.
Correct. The Internet has no central control; each network owner manages their own part.

hint: Who 'owns' the Internet?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The Internet is a **decentralised** global network of networks. Owners of the various parts maintain them, and nobody checks content before it is published. This is exactly why users must **evaluate** information (authority, accuracy, currency, reliability) before using it academically.

## Simplified explanation

Anyone can publish online and **no one checks it first**, so the statement is false.

body: Which step in the search strategy will you be considering **search tools** to use in your search? Step _______.

options.hint: Step 2 is choosing your search terms.
Correct. Step 3 is deciding which sources or search tools to use.
Step 4 is finding out how the chosen search tool functions.
Step 5 is running the search.

hint: Define need → choose terms → … ?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The six steps taught in ILT 101: 1. Define your information need. 2. Choose your search terms. 3. **Decide which sources/search tools to use**. 4. Find out how the search tool functions. 5. Run your search. 6. Review and refine your search. Steps 1–3 can be done away from the computer.

## Simplified explanation

You first know **what** you want (1), pick **keywords** (2), then pick **where** to search (3).

body: The asterisk (`*`) sign is used in _______ searching.

options.hint: Boolean searching uses AND, OR, NOT.
Browsing is following links or categories, not a symbol.
Phrase searching uses quotation marks, e.g. "information literacy".
Correct. The asterisk is the truncation/wildcard symbol.

hint: `educat*` finds educate, education, educational…
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Truncation/wildcard** searching uses a symbol (usually `*`) to stand for any ending: `librar*` retrieves _library_, _libraries_, _librarian_. It widens a search to word variants without typing each one.

## Simplified explanation

The `*` means 'anything can follow here', so one search catches many word forms.

body: The _______ Boolean operator allows **either** of the keywords to be present in each record in the results.

options.hint: AND requires both keywords in every record; it narrows the search.
NOT excludes records containing a keyword.
NONE is not a Boolean operator.
Correct. OR accepts records with either keyword (or both); it broadens the search.

hint: Which operator makes results bigger?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Boolean operators: **AND** (both terms → fewer results), **OR** (either term → more results; used for synonyms such as `teenagers OR adolescents`), **NOT** (exclude a term → fewer results).

## Simplified explanation

**OR** = this one _or_ that one, so you get more results.

body: Any information source that provides access to information in an electronic format is a/an _______.

options.hint: A database is one kind of electronic source, a collection of structured records.
Correct. 'Electronic source' covers any source delivering information electronically.
Email is a communication service.
A search engine is a retrieval tool, not every electronic source.

hint: The answer is the general term, not one example.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

An **electronic (e-)source** is the umbrella term for any resource accessed in electronic format: databases, e-journals, e-books, websites, CD-ROMs. A **database** is one specific type (structured records allowing orderly retrieval).

## Simplified explanation

The question asks for the **general name**. All e-books, e-journals and databases are electronic sources.

body: Research on the Internet is the same as research in the traditional library.

options.hint: Library materials are selected and organised; Internet content is not.
Correct. Library collections are selected, catalogued and classified; the Web is not indexed or controlled.

hint: Who checks and organises what is on the Web?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Library materials are **selected, catalogued and classified** by professionals, so retrieval is systematic. The Web is not indexed or catalogued as a whole, has no central control, and quality varies. Researching online therefore needs a **search strategy** and **evaluation** of sources.

## Simplified explanation

In the library someone has already checked and arranged the books. Online, **you** must do that work, so it is not the same.

body: The Internet is a network of _______ spanning the globe.

options.hint: Communication is a use of the Internet, not what it is made of.
Correct. The Internet is a global network of computer networks.
Messages travel over the Internet; they do not make it up.
People use the Internet, but the network is of computers.

hint: What physically links together?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The Internet is **a global network of computer networks**, linking millions of computers in businesses, government agencies, institutions and homes, communicating by TCP/IP.

## Simplified explanation

The Internet joins **computers** all over the world.

body: The Internet is centrally controlled by a body of government agencies.

options.hint: No government body controls the whole Internet.
Correct. The Internet has no central control.

hint: Same idea as 'no centralized monitor'.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The Internet is **not centrally controlled**: the owners of each part maintain their own networks. Standards bodies coordinate technical rules (protocols, domain names), but nobody controls content.

## Simplified explanation

No government runs the whole Internet, so this is **false**.

body: Which is **NOT** a resource shared on computer networks?

options.hint: Data (files, databases) is shared on networks.
Hardware such as printers and scanners is shared.
Software and applications can be shared from a server.
Correct. Physical space is not a network resource.

hint: Networks share information and electronic resources.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **computer network** is a group of computers connected to share **information and electronic resources**: data, hardware (printers, storage) and software. Physical _space_ is not something a network shares.

## Simplified explanation

Networks share **files, printers and programs**. Not room space.

body: Which of the uses does **video and audio conferencing** fall under?

options.hint: Correct. Conferencing is real-time communication between people.
It can be used in teaching, but it is classified as communication.
It is not mainly for entertainment.
It is not a research activity in itself.

hint: Talking and seeing each other live.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Under **communication** the notes list email, instant messaging, VoIP, social networking, and **audio/video conferencing**, all used to exchange messages in real time.

## Simplified explanation

Video calls are people **talking** to each other, which is communication.

body: Which is a function of a **computer virus**?

options.hint: Correct of these options: many viruses spy on or steal private data while disrupting the system.
This is not a recognised virus function.
Networks transmit data; that is normal, not malicious.
Storing information is what disks do.

hint: What harm does malware do to users?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **computer virus** is a program or code that disrupts the normal functioning of a computer when loaded onto it. Viruses corrupt or delete files, slow systems and are often used to **access private information** (passwords, banking details), which links to identity theft.

## Simplified explanation

A virus is a harmful program. Among the options, the harmful act is **spying on private information**.

body: Sending unsolicited and unwanted bulk messages is known as _______.

options.hint: Spam is a misuse of communication channels.
Dissemination is spreading information generally.
Fraud is deception for gain; spam may carry fraud but is defined by bulk unsolicited messages.
Correct. Unsolicited bulk email or messages is spam.

hint: The junk folder in your email.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Spamming** is sending unsolicited, unwanted messages in bulk, usually advertising, sometimes carrying viruses or phishing links. It is listed among the **misuses** of the Internet with identity theft, pornography and virus threats.

## Simplified explanation

Junk messages sent to many people you never asked to hear from are **spam**.

body: _______ are automated software applications that travel along the web.

options.hint: Databases store records; they do not travel the web.
Directories are human-organised lists of websites.
Search engines use these programs, but the programs themselves are…
Correct. Spiders (robots or crawlers) automatically visit pages for search engines.

hint: They 'crawl' the web like insects.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Search engines are made up of **spiders** (robots or crawlers) that automatically travel the web collecting pages, an **index** of what they collect, and a **search interface**.

## Simplified explanation

**Spiders** are programs that crawl from page to page to feed the search engine.

body: In evaluating Internet resources, which of the under-listed checklist will you be applying when you consider the **trustworthiness** of the source?

options.hint: Accuracy is whether facts are correct and complete.
Correct. Credibility is about how far the source can be trusted.
Currency is how up to date it is.
Relevance is how well it meets your need.

hint: Trust = ?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The evaluation criteria in the notes: reliability, authority, **credibility**, accuracy/completeness, relevancy and currency. **Credibility** asks whether the source deserves belief: the author's credentials, expertise and association with a credible institution.

## Simplified explanation

Trustworthy = **credible**.

body: Bandwidth is measured in _______.

options.hint: Kilo is only a prefix, not a unit.
Storage is usually counted in bytes; bandwidth in bits.
Correct. Bandwidth is measured in bits per second (bps).
Hertz measures frequency.

hint: Note the difference between bits and bytes.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bandwidth is measured in **bits per second** (`bps`), usually `kbps` or `Mbps`. Note: `1 byte = 8 bits`, so a `10 Mbps` line downloads about `1.25 MB` per second.

## Simplified explanation

Internet speed is counted in **bits per second**.

> [!warning]
> Do not confuse `Mbps` (megabits, speed) with `MB` (megabytes, file size).

body: The internet is centrally controlled by the _______.

options.hint: This body publishes security guidance; it does not control the Internet.
It regulates Ghana's media, not the Internet as a whole.
No such body controls the Internet.
Correct. The Internet has no central controller.

hint: Is anyone in charge of the whole Internet?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The Internet has **no central control**. Each network owner maintains their own part, which is why its information must be evaluated before academic use.

## Simplified explanation

Nobody owns or controls the whole Internet, so **none of the above**.

body: A reference source helpful in learning **specific vocabulary** is a _______.

options.hint: Correct. A thesaurus groups words with related meanings (synonyms) and controlled terms.
A journal is a periodical of articles.
A textbook teaches a subject, not vocabulary lists.
A directory lists people or organisations with contact details.

hint: Where do you find synonyms?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **thesaurus** is a reference source of words or terms grouped by meaning (synonyms, related and broader/narrower terms). It helps you find **specific vocabulary**, and in searching it supplies alternative keywords.

## Simplified explanation

Need another word for something? Use a **thesaurus**.

body: _______ work is any work based on an already copyrighted work.

options.hint: There is no such category.
Too general: any protected work is copyrighted.
Correct. A derivative work adapts an existing work, e.g. a translation or film adaptation.
Public-domain works have no copyright protection.

hint: Translations, adaptations, arrangements…
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **derivative work** is built on an existing work: translations, film or stage adaptations, musical arrangements. The copyright owner has the exclusive right to determine who may **adapt** the work into such derivative forms.

## Simplified explanation

If you make something new **from** someone else's work (like translating their book), it is a **derivative** work.

body: You must cite your source if _______.

options.hint: True, but it is not the only case.
True. Paraphrased ideas also need citing.
True. Online sources must be cited too.
Correct. Quotations, paraphrased ideas and web sources all require citation.

hint: Is any of these cases exempt?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Citation is needed whenever you use someone else's **words, ideas, data or media**, whether quoted directly, **paraphrased**, or taken from print or **web** sources. Only common knowledge and your own original ideas need no citation.

## Simplified explanation

If it came from someone else, in any form, **cite it**.

body: The main reason for citing sources is to _______.

options.hint: Correct. Citation acknowledges the owner of the words or ideas.
A side benefit, not the main reason.
Not the purpose of citation.
Citations do let readers find sources, but the core reason is acknowledgement.

hint: Avoiding plagiarism is about acknowledging ownership.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Citing **acknowledges the original author** and so avoids plagiarism. It also lets readers locate the source and verify claims, and shows the scholarship behind your work.

## Simplified explanation

You cite to **give credit** to the person whose work you used.

body: Library service that provides quick help to users is called _______ service.

options.hint: Lending is borrowing materials out.
Correct. Reference service answers users' questions and guides them to information.
This gives access to e-resources.
This teaches users to use the library, e.g. orientation.

hint: The help desk in the library.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Reference service** is the personal help librarians give at the reference desk: answering quick factual questions and guiding users to the right sources.

## Simplified explanation

The librarian at the desk who answers your questions is giving **reference service**.

body: The following are advantages of **broadband** except _______.

options.hint: This is an advantage of broadband.
This is an advantage of broadband.
Correct. 'Fast passwords' is not a feature of broadband.
Always-on fast links make remote administration possible.

hint: Which option is not about connection speed at all?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Broadband is a generic term for **faster, always-on** Internet connections (DSL, cable modem, satellite modem, wireless, mobile broadband). Its advantages are fast browsing and downloads, multimedia streaming and remote administration. 'Fast passwords' is meaningless here.

## Simplified explanation

Broadband makes things **load faster**. It has nothing to do with passwords.

body: MARC stands for _______.

options.hint: Close, but the standard is singular: Machine-Readable Cataloguing/Catalogue.
'Automated' is not part of the name.
Correct. MARC is the Machine-Readable Cataloguing standard.
'Accessible' is not part of the name.

hint: M-A-R-C, four words.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**MARC** (`Machine-Readable Cataloguing`) is the standard format for encoding catalogue records so computers can store, exchange and display them. It underlies **OPACs**.

## Simplified explanation

MARC is how a catalogue record is written so a **machine can read** it.

body: Information literacy helps individuals become _______.

options.hint: Not related to information literacy.
Not the stated outcome.
That needs professional training such as librarianship.
Correct. Information literacy produces effective, ethical information users.

hint: The goal of ILT 101 for every student.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Information literacy is the ability to recognise an information need and to **find, evaluate and use information effectively and ethically** (the ACRL standards). Its outcome is a **good information user**, not necessarily an information professional.

## Simplified explanation

The course makes you **good at finding and using information**.

body: _______ are doorways used to trace materials in a catalogue.

options.hint: Not the standard term.
Not the standard term.
Correct. Access points (author, title, subject, call mark, series, ISBN) lead to records.
Not the standard term.

hint: Author, title, subject…
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Access points** are the codes or terms used to locate a record in a catalogue or database: **call mark, author, title, subject, series and ISBN**.

## Simplified explanation

They are the 'ways in' to a record, so **access points**.

body: The main goal of a National Library is bibliographic control of materials published in a _______.

options.hint: Incomplete: it also covers works about the country.
Colonies are not part of the mandate.
Correct. It controls works published in the country and works about it.
Not its mandate.

hint: Think of George Padmore Library's mandate.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A national library ensures **bibliographic control of all materials published in the country _and_ about the country**, through legal deposit and compiling the national bibliography. In Ghana, the **George Padmore Research Library on African Affairs** plays this role.

## Simplified explanation

It keeps a record of everything published **in** Ghana and **about** Ghana.

body: A network covering **Cape Coast and its environs** is a _______.

options.hint: A LAN covers one building.
A CAN covers one campus.
Correct. A Metropolitan Area Network covers a city or town.
A WAN covers countries or continents.

hint: City-sized network.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**MAN** (Metropolitan Area Network) spans a city or metropolis such as Cape Coast and its surroundings: bigger than a campus (CAN), smaller than a WAN.

## Simplified explanation

City = **Metropolitan** Area Network.

body: The citation style used in the University of Cape Coast is _______.

options.hint: MLA is used in the humanities (languages and literature).
Correct. UCC adopts the APA style.
AMA is used in medicine.
ASA is used in sociology.

hint: The style you practise in every ILT 101 exam.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

UCC uses the **American Psychological Association (APA)** style: author–date in-text citations `(Mensah, 2020)` and an alphabetical reference list. MLA (Modern Language Association) is the other style taught, mainly for the humanities.

## Simplified explanation

UCC uses **APA**.

body: The _Daily Graphic_ is **not** an example of periodicals.

options.hint: The Daily Graphic is a newspaper, which is a periodical.
Correct. Newspapers appear at regular intervals under one title, so they are periodicals.

hint: Does it appear regularly under one title?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **periodical** is a serial publication with a distinctive title appearing at regular or irregular intervals, generally more than once a year, with no planned last issue. The notes even give _The Mirror_ (a weekly newspaper) as an example. The _Daily Graphic_ fits, so the statement is **false**.

## Simplified explanation

The Daily Graphic comes out **every day** with the same title, so it **is** a periodical.

body: Which reference material helps in **introducing a guest speaker**?

options.hint: Gives topic overviews, not personal life histories.
Gives names and contact details only.
Lists publications.
Correct. Biographical sources give a person's life history and achievements.

hint: You need facts about a person's life and achievements.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Biographical sources** (universal, national, regional biographies, _Who's Who_) give life histories, positions and achievements of people. That is exactly what you need to introduce a speaker.

## Simplified explanation

To introduce someone you need their **life story**, which is in a **biography**.

body: Information in reference materials is arranged systematically to ensure _______.

options.hint: Correct. Systematic arrangement lets users find facts quickly.
A by-product, not the purpose.
Not the main purpose.
Arrangement does not make information accurate.

hint: Reference books are consulted, not read cover to cover.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Reference materials are **consulted** for specific facts, so their content is arranged alphabetically, tabularly, regionally, chronologically or by classification to give **easy, quick access**.

## Simplified explanation

They are arranged in order so you can **find things fast**.

body: All the features of a traditional library may be present in a hybrid library.

options.hint: Correct. A hybrid library keeps print collections and services and adds electronic ones.
A hybrid library includes the traditional (print) side.

hint: Hybrid = print + electronic.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **hybrid library** holds information in both **print and non-print (electronic)** formats; users have physical and electronic access, e.g. through an OPAC. It therefore contains a traditional library's features plus digital ones. Most academic libraries, such as UCC's Sam Jonah Library, are hybrid.

## Simplified explanation

Hybrid means **both**: everything traditional, plus digital.

body: Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC) is commonly used in _______ libraries.

options.hint: Many academic and research libraries use Library of Congress (LC).
Not the usual pairing.
Academic libraries more commonly use LC.
Correct. DDC is typical of public and school libraries.

hint: LC is usually for big academic libraries.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The two major schemes: **Dewey Decimal Classification** (numbers `000–999`, e.g. `020` Library science), common in **public and school** libraries; and **Library of Congress** (letters, e.g. `Z` Bibliography), common in **academic and research** libraries such as UCC's.

## Simplified explanation

Smaller public and school libraries use **Dewey**; university libraries use **LC**.

body: There are _______ different types of libraries.

options.hint: Three is the number of forms (traditional, digital, hybrid), not types.
Too few.
Correct. Academic, public, school, special and national.
Five is correct.

hint: Academic, public, school…
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

ILT 101 distinguishes **five types** of libraries by the users they serve: **academic, public, school, special and national**. Separately, there are three **forms**: traditional, digital/electronic and hybrid.

## Simplified explanation

Five types: academic, public, school, special, national.

> [!warning]
> Do not mix up **types** (five) with **forms** (three).

body: Librarians acquire, catalogue, classify and arrange materials in a library to provide _______.

options.hint: Alerts are a separate service (SDI).
Display is not the purpose of cataloguing.
Correct. Organising knowledge makes materials easy to find.
Preservation is a different function.

hint: Why catalogue and classify at all?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cataloguing and classification are the **tools for organising knowledge**: they let users find an item by author, title or subject, see what the library holds, and choose an edition. The overall aim is **easy retrieval**.

## Simplified explanation

Everything is put in order so you can **find it easily**.

body: Materials such as email and PowerPoint files that are created or originate in a digital form are termed _______.

options.hint: Not the standard term.
Digitised materials started as print and were scanned or converted.
Correct. Born-digital materials were created digitally from the start.
Not a term.

hint: Where did the material start life?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Digital libraries hold two kinds of material: **born digital** (created digitally: MS Office files, images, audio, video from cameras and computers) and **digitised** (created in print or analogue form, then converted by scanning).

## Simplified explanation

If it was **created on a computer** from the start, it is **born digital**.

body: These are all examples of **special libraries** except _______.

options.hint: A special (research institute) library.
A special (research institute) library.

options.text: George Padmore Research Library on African Affairs
options.hint: Correct. It serves as Ghana's National Library.
A special (government) library.

hint: Which one plays a national role?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Special libraries** serve staff of government, research, commercial and business organisations: Supreme Court Library, Animal Research Institute, Crops Research Institute, Oil Palm Research Institute and so on. **George Padmore Research Library on African Affairs** functions as Ghana's **national library**.

## Simplified explanation

All are research or government libraries **except Padmore**, which is the national library.

body: Abstracting, indexing and Selective Dissemination of Information are special services performed by a _______.

options.hint: Public libraries focus on lending and community services.
School libraries support school programmes.
Academic libraries offer some of these, but they are typical of special libraries.
Correct. Special libraries serve specialist staff with SDI, indexing and abstracting.

hint: Which library serves researchers in an organisation?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Special libraries** give value-added services to their specialist users: **SDI** (alerting each user to new publications in their field), **indexing** and **abstracting**.

## Simplified explanation

These tailored research services are typical of **special** libraries.

body: International Standard Serial Number (ISSN) and International Standard Book Number (ISBN) are managed by the _______.

options.hint: Correct. The national library assigns ISBN/ISSN as part of bibliographic control.
Not their role.

options.text: George Padmore Research Library on African Affairs
options.hint: This is Ghana's national library, but the general answer is 'national library'.
Not their role.

hint: Which library controls a country's publishing output?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

As part of **bibliographic control**, the **national library** runs the ISBN (books) and ISSN (serials) agencies, receives legal-deposit copies and compiles the national bibliography.

## Simplified explanation

Numbering every book and journal published in a country is the **national library**'s job.

body: George Padmore Research Library on African Affairs in Ghana functions as a _______.

options.hint: Not its function.
Not its function.
True, but it is also more.
True, but it is also more.
Correct. It is both a research library on African affairs and Ghana's national library.
Not its function.

hint: Two of the options are both true.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **George Padmore Research Library on African Affairs** is a research library specialising in African affairs, and it **serves as the National Library of Ghana** (legal deposit, national bibliography, ISBN/ISSN).

## Simplified explanation

It does **both** jobs: African-affairs library **and** national library.

body: A library that harnesses the advantages of all other forms or categories of libraries is _______.

options.hint: Only electronic.
Only print, operated manually.
Correct. It combines print and electronic resources and services.
