body: **Define** _Information Literacy_.
answer:
**Information literacy** is the body of **knowledge, skills, competencies and understanding** required by an individual to **find information effectively and use it appropriately** to meet the need that prompted its acquisition.

_Alternative (also accepted):_ the ability to use techniques and skills from a wide range of information tools, as well as primary sources, in moulding information solutions to problems.

> [!answer]
> Information literacy = the skills to **recognise** an information need, then **find, evaluate and use** information effectively and ethically.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The term was coined by **Paul Zurkowski (1974)**. The **ACRL** (Association of College & Research Libraries) defines it as the set of abilities requiring individuals to _recognise when information is needed and have the ability to locate, evaluate, and use effectively the needed information_. It is the foundation for lifelong learning in an age of information overload.

## Simplified explanation

Being information literate means you **know when you need information**, know **where to find it**, can **tell good from bad**, and **use it honestly** (with citations).

> [!tip]
> Two-mark definitions: use the key verbs **find**, **evaluate**, **use** + **effectively/appropriately**.
hint: Your definition should cover finding information **and** using it appropriately.

body: State **four (4)** reasons why students should be information literate. _(Also asked: three importance of information literacy to a university student; the benefits of the Information Literacy Skills course to a university graduate.)_
answer:
1. **To recognise when information is needed** and define the need clearly.
2. **To locate where the information is**, using the library catalogue, databases and the Internet efficiently.
3. **To evaluate information critically**, separating reliable, authoritative sources from false or biased ones, especially online.
4. **To use information effectively, efficiently and ethically**: citing sources, avoiding plagiarism and respecting copyright.
5. **For decision making and productivity**, which benefits the individual and society.
6. **For lifelong learning and employability**: graduates who can find and judge information keep learning after school.

> [!answer]
> Any four: recognise need · locate information · evaluate it · use it ethically · decision making · lifelong learning.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These reasons mirror the **five ACRL standards** (know, access, evaluate, use, ethical/legal). For a graduate the course's benefits go beyond school: **critical thinking**, **research competence** for projects and theses, **academic integrity**, and the **transferable skill** of learning independently in an information-rich, misinformation-prone environment.

## Simplified explanation

There is too much information today, and much of it is wrong. Information-literate students know **what they need, where to get it, whether it is true, and how to use it honestly**.
hint: Follow the life cycle of information: need → find → judge → use.

body: Using the **five (5) standards** of the _Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL)_, explain who an information literate person is. _(Also asked: What makes a student information literate? / Write short notes on the five ACRL standards / List two ACRL standards.)_
answer:
An information literate person is one who:

| # | ACRL standard | What the person can do |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **To know** | _Determines the nature and extent_ of the information needed. |
| 2 | **To access** | _Accesses the needed information effectively and efficiently_ (search tools, catalogue, databases). |
| 3 | **To evaluate** | _Evaluates information and its sources critically_ and incorporates selected information into their knowledge base. |
| 4 | **To use** | _Uses information effectively_ to accomplish a specific purpose. |
| 5 | **Ethical/Legal** | _Understands the economic, legal and social issues_ around information and **accesses and uses it ethically and legally** (copyright, citation, no plagiarism). |

> [!answer]
> Know · Access · Evaluate · Use · Ethical/Legal use.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The ACRL _Information Literacy Competency Standards for Higher Education_ (2000) turn information literacy into measurable outcomes. Each standard has performance indicators. Under **standard 3**, for example, the student applies criteria such as **authority, accuracy, objectivity, currency and coverage**; under **standard 5**, the student follows copyright law and **acknowledges sources**. Write each standard as a sentence describing the person, for 2 marks each.

## Simplified explanation

Picture a good researcher. They **know** what they want, can **get** it, can **judge** it, can **use** it, and do so **honestly**. Those are the five standards.

> [!tip]
> Memory hook: **K-A-E-U-E**, 'Know, Access, Evaluate, Use, Ethically'.
hint: Five verbs: know, access, evaluate, use, and use ethically.

body: Name the **five (5) types** of libraries.
answer:
1. **Academic library**: college/university libraries (e.g. Sam Jonah Library, UCC)
2. **Public library**: serves the general public (Ghana Library Authority)
3. **School library**: in pre-tertiary schools
4. **Special library**: in government, research, business organisations (e.g. Supreme Court Library)
5. **National library**: bibliographic control for the nation (George Padmore Research Library on African Affairs)

> [!answer]
> Academic · Public · School · Special · National.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Libraries are typed by **clientele and function**. Each type can exist in any **form** (traditional, digital, hybrid). Academic libraries support teaching, learning and research; public libraries serve communities; school libraries support pre-tertiary curricula; special libraries meet the specialised needs of an organisation's staff; national libraries carry out legal deposit and bibliographic control.

## Simplified explanation

Ask: **who uses it?** University people → academic. Everyone → public. Pupils → school. Staff of an organisation → special. The whole nation → national.

> [!warning]
> Traditional, digital and hybrid are **forms**, not types.
hint: Types are classified by the **users** each library serves.

body: Name the **forms or categories** of libraries and write on any **two (2)** of them.
answer:
**Forms/categories:** **traditional**, **digital/electronic** and **hybrid** libraries.

**1. Traditional library:** most operations are done **manually**, without the aid of computer technology; resources are mainly in **print**.
- _Advantages:_ stable collection; free and universal access; no computer expertise required; usable without electricity; documents can be photocopied.
- _Disadvantages:_ centralised management; limited access; slow update of collections; users limited to the physical location; contents not linked to each other.

**2. Digital/electronic library:** **all information resources and services are in digital form**: born-digital and digitised materials accessed through computers and networks.
- _Advantages:_ access anywhere, any time; quicker access; easy sharing with other digital libraries; direct use of the documents found.
- _Disadvantages:_ needs electricity and adequate bandwidth; expensive to set up and manage; content may not be well screened; hard to locate everything without computer literacy.

**3. Hybrid library:** holds information in **both print and non-print formats**; users have physical and electronic access, e.g. through an **OPAC**. Most academic libraries are hybrid (Sam Jonah Library UCC, Balme Library Legon, Prempeh II Library KNUST).

> [!answer]
> Forms: traditional, digital/electronic, hybrid. Describe two with features, advantages and disadvantages.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **form** of a library is independent of its **type**: a public library can be traditional and an academic library can be hybrid. The trend in Ghana is towards **hybrid** libraries: they keep the stability and universality of print and add the reach of e-resources (e-journals, databases, institutional repositories).

## Simplified explanation

**Traditional** = books on shelves, done by hand. **Digital** = everything on computers. **Hybrid** = both, like UCC's library.
hint: Forms describe **how** information is held and served: manually, digitally, or both.

body: Discuss **five (5)** reasons why you would recommend one of the types of libraries to your friend in another university.
answer:
_I would recommend the **academic library**._

1. **Supports the curriculum:** its collection reflects the academic programmes of the university, so the textbooks and references a student needs are there.
2. **Access to e-resources:** subscribed databases and e-journals (JSTOR, SAGE, Emerald, AGORA) that a student cannot get free on the open web.
3. **Reference service:** librarians answer queries and guide students to the right sources for assignments and theses.
4. **User education:** orientation and information literacy training improve students' searching, evaluation and citation skills.
5. **Inter-library loan and document delivery (ILL/DD):** materials not held locally can be obtained from other libraries.
6. **Conducive study environment:** reading rooms, carrels, Wi-Fi and computers for quiet, extended study.
7. **Reprographic services:** photocopying, scanning and printing of needed materials (within copyright limits).

> [!answer]
> Choose one type (e.g. **academic library**) and give five supported reasons: relevant collection, e-resources, reference help, user education, ILL/DD, study space.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Marks (3 each) come from **stating a reason _and_ explaining its value** to the friend. The academic library is the natural choice: accreditation bodies judge programmes partly on whether the library's collection supports the curriculum, and it is the hub for scholarly databases a student cannot reach elsewhere.

## Simplified explanation

Tell your friend: _'Use the university library, because it has the books for **your** course, online journals, helpful librarians, training, and a quiet place to study.'_
hint: Pick the type that best fits a university student, then argue from its services.

body: Write short notes on any **two (2)** of the following: (i) **School library**, (ii) **Public library**, (iii) **Academic library**.
answer:
**School library:** a library within a **pre-tertiary institution**, used by pupils/students and staff of a public or private school. It **supports the school's educational programmes**. Its collection includes general reference materials, textbooks and novels for lending, and non-print materials (films, audio/video recordings, computers, CD-ROMs).

**Public library:** serves the **general public** of a community, district or region **without restriction**, irrespective of age, education or status. It supports literacy, recreation, self-education and community information. In Ghana public libraries are run by the **Ghana Library Authority**. It is the type most familiar and visible to people.

**Academic library:** a **college or university** library used by academic staff, researchers, students and administrators. It **supports teaching, learning and research**. Its collection reflects the institution's programmes: reference books, textbooks, periodicals, newspapers, government publications and a wide range of **electronic resources**. Adequacy of its collection is a criterion for **accrediting** academic programmes. Example: Sam Jonah Library, UCC.

> [!answer]
> For each: who it serves, its purpose, its collection, and an example.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A strong short note (5–6 marks) covers **definition, clientele, function, collection and an example**. Differentiate clearly: _school_ supports pre-tertiary curricula, _public_ serves the whole community without restriction, _academic_ supports teaching, learning **and research** and is tied to accreditation.

## Simplified explanation

School library = for pupils. Public library = for everybody in town. Academic library = for a university, including research.
hint: Structure each note: **users → purpose → collection → example**.

body: (a) What is an **academic library**? (b) Describe the **facilities and services** of an academic library using the **UCC Library** as an example.
answer:
**(a)** An academic library is the library of a **college or university**, established to **support the teaching, learning and research** activities of its parent institution, serving students, academic staff, researchers and administrators.

**(b) Facilities** (Sam Jonah Library, UCC):
- **Reading rooms** and study carrels; group discussion rooms
- **ICT facilities**: computer labs/e-library, campus Wi-Fi, OPAC terminals
- Separate **sections**: reference, lending/circulation, periodicals/serials, special collections (e.g. theses, Africana)
- **Reprographic** equipment: photocopiers, scanners, printers

**Services:**
- **Lending/circulation** of books
- **Reference service**: help desk and research consultation
- **Electronic support**: access to subscribed databases and e-journals (JSTOR, SAGE, Emerald, Research4Life) and the institutional repository
- **Inter-library loan and document delivery (ILL/DD)**
- **User education**: orientation for fresh students, library tours, information literacy training
- **Reprographic** services

> [!answer]
> An academic library supports teaching, learning and research; describe UCC's facilities (reading rooms, ICT, sections) and services (lending, reference, e-resources, ILL/DD, user education, reprography).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Examiners reward **concrete UCC examples**. Link each service to its purpose: lending extends use beyond opening hours; e-resources give access to peer-reviewed literature; user education builds the ACRL competencies; ILL/DD overcomes the limits of any single collection.

## Simplified explanation

Describe what you actually see and use in the UCC library: **study spaces, computers, books to borrow, librarians who help, online journals, orientation and photocopying**.
hint: Split your answer into **facilities** (what is there) and **services** (what is done for users).

body: Explain **four (4)** library services and indicate **two (2)** types of libraries that undertake each. _(Also asked: list five services of an academic library; explain any four library services.)_
answer:
| Service | Explanation | Libraries that offer it |
|---|---|---|
| **Lending (circulation)** | Users borrow materials for use outside the library for a set period. | Public, academic, school |
| **Reference service** | Librarians answer queries and direct users to appropriate sources. | Academic, public, special |
| **Inter-library loan & document delivery (ILL/DD)** | Obtaining materials from other libraries for users; copies sent are for permanent retention. | Academic, special |
| **Electronic support** | Access to resources in electronic format: databases, e-journals, CD-ROMs, Internet. | Academic, special, national |
| **Reprographic service** | Photocopying, scanning and printing of materials for users. | Academic, public |
| **User education** | Orientation for fresh students, library tours and information literacy instruction. | Academic, school |
| **Selective Dissemination of Information (SDI)** | Customised alerting of users to new publications in their field. | Special, academic |

> [!answer]
> Any four services with an explanation and two library types each, e.g. lending (public, academic), reference (academic, special), ILL/DD (academic, special), user education (academic, school).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Services differ with clientele. **Special libraries** emphasise value-added, current-awareness services (SDI, indexing, abstracting) for specialist staff; **academic libraries** offer the widest range, especially e-resource support and user education; **public libraries** concentrate on lending, reference and community programmes.

## Simplified explanation

A library service is anything the library **does for you**: lends books, answers questions, gets books from other libraries, gives online access, photocopies, trains you.
hint: Use a three-column layout: service · what it is · who offers it.

body: Write short notes on the following library services: (i) **Abstracting services** (ii) **Indexing services** (iii) **Selective Dissemination of Information (SDI)** (iv) **Interlibrary loan and document delivery (ILL/DD)** (v) **User education**.
answer:
- **Abstracting service:** provides the **full bibliographic details** of documents **and a brief summary** of their subject content, so users can judge relevance without reading the whole document. Types: _informative_ and _indicative_ abstracts.
- **Indexing service:** provides the **bibliographic details** (author, title, source, volume, pages) of articles and reports, arranged for retrieval, but **without a summary**.
- **SDI:** a **customised alerting service** whereby users are regularly updated on **new publications related to their field** of study or research interest, based on their profiles. Typical of special libraries.
- **ILL/DD:** an arrangement by which a library **borrows materials from, or obtains copies from, other libraries** for its users; copies sent are usually for permanent retention.
- **User education:** programmes that **teach users how to use the library** and its resources effectively: orientation for fresh students, library tours, and information literacy instruction.

> [!answer]
> Abstracting = details + summary; indexing = details only; SDI = personalised alerts; ILL/DD = getting materials from other libraries; user education = teaching users to use the library.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Indexing and abstracting are **secondary (directional) services** that point to primary literature. SDI is a **current-awareness** service matching new items to stored **user profiles** (today often automated as database alerts). ILL/DD extends access beyond one collection, and user education builds the competencies of the ACRL standards.

## Simplified explanation

**Index** tells you where an article is; an **abstract** also tells you what it says. **SDI** is the library sending you news on your topic. **ILL** is borrowing from another library. **User education** is library training.
hint: Show the difference between indexing and abstracting.

body: List **five (5)** functions of a **National library**.
answer:
1. **Legal deposit:** receives, free of charge, at least one copy of every work published in the country.
2. **Compilation of the national bibliography.**
3. **Storage of numerous valuable works and rare books**: preserving the nation's documentary heritage.
4. **Practical training** for library personnel.
5. **Conducting research** as a consultancy service for individuals and the nation.
6. **Allocation of ISBN and ISSN** to publications.

> [!answer]
> Legal deposit · national bibliography · preservation of rare/valuable works · training of library staff · research/consultancy (· ISBN/ISSN).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

All these serve one goal: **universal bibliographic control**, i.e. ensuring every publication **in and about** the country is collected, recorded and preserved. In Ghana this role is played by the **George Padmore Research Library on African Affairs**. Legal deposit supplies the collection; the national bibliography and ISBN/ISSN give the records.

## Simplified explanation

The national library is the country's **memory**: it keeps a copy of everything published, lists it, numbers it, preserves it, and trains librarians.
hint: Its main goal is bibliographic control of everything published in and about the country.

body: (a) What is a **traditional library**? (b) State **four (4)** advantages of a traditional library.
answer:
**(a)** A traditional library is one where **most operations are done manually, without the aid of computer technology**, and resources are mainly in **print** format.

**(b) Advantages:**
1. **Stable collection**: materials do not disappear like web pages.
2. **Free and universal access** to the collection.
3. **No computer expertise** is required of staff or users.
4. **Can be used without electricity.**
5. **Documents can easily be photocopied.**

> [!answer]
> Manual, print-based library; advantages: stable collection, free/universal access, no computer skills needed, works without electricity, easy photocopying.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The traditional library's strengths are **permanence and inclusiveness**: a printed book stays put, and anyone can use it without devices, power or digital skills. That matters in contexts with unreliable electricity or bandwidth. Its weaknesses (slow updates, physical limits) are what digital and hybrid libraries address.

## Simplified explanation

A traditional library is **books on shelves, done by hand**. Good because anyone can use it, even without light or Internet, and the books do not vanish.
hint: Think about what still works when there is no power or Internet.

body: State **five (5)** disadvantages of a **traditional library**.
answer:
1. **Centralised management** of resources.
2. **Limited access** to materials: only a few users can use a copy at a time.
3. **Slow update** of the collection.
4. **Users are limited to the physical location** and opening hours.
5. **Contents of materials are not directly linked** with each other (no hyperlinks or full-text search).

> [!answer]
> Centralised management · limited access · slow updates · tied to location and hours · no links between contents.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These limitations come from **physical media**: one printed copy serves one user at one place, new editions take time to acquire and process, and print cannot be searched across documents. Digital and hybrid libraries answer them with remote, simultaneous access and linked, searchable content.

## Simplified explanation

You must **go there**, during **opening hours**, and hope the **one copy** is not borrowed. Books are also slow to be replaced.
hint: Compare with what a digital library can do.

body: State **five (5)** advantages of a **digital library**.
answer:
1. **Information can be accessed anywhere and at any time.**
2. **Quicker access** to information through computers and networks.
3. **Information is easily shared** with other digital libraries.
4. **Users can directly access and use** the documents found (full text).
5. **Multiple users** can use the same item **simultaneously**.
6. **Saves physical space** and reduces wear of materials.

> [!answer]
> Anytime/anywhere access · speed · easy sharing · direct full-text use · simultaneous users · saves space.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Digital libraries remove the **constraints of place, time and copies**. Born-digital and digitised resources can be searched in full text, linked, shared across institutions and used by many people at once, supporting distance learners (e.g. CoDE students).

## Simplified explanation

With a digital library you can read **from anywhere, at any time**, quickly, even if others are reading the same item.
hint: Think of using the library from your hostel at midnight.

body: List **five (5)** disadvantages of **digital libraries**.
answer:
1. **Cannot be used without electricity** and adequate **bandwidth**.
2. **More expensive to set up and manage** (hardware, software, licences, skilled staff).
3. **Content may not be well screened and validated.**
4. **Difficulty knowing and locating** everything available, and separating valuable from useless information, for users who are **not computer literate**.
5. **Job loss** for traditional publishers.

> [!answer]
> Needs power and bandwidth · costly · unscreened content · hard for non-computer-literate users · job losses in publishing.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The weaknesses are **infrastructural** (power, bandwidth, devices), **economic** (licences, maintenance, digital preservation) and **human** (digital literacy, quality control). In Ghana, erratic power supply and data costs make these especially relevant, which is one reason hybrid libraries are preferred.

## Simplified explanation

No **power** or **data**, no library. It is also **expensive**, and some content is **not checked**.
hint: What does a digital library depend on that a book does not?

body: State **two (2)** disadvantages of a **hybrid library**.
answer:
1. **High cost**: the library must maintain **both** print collections and electronic infrastructure (licences, hardware, maintenance).
2. **Dependence on electricity, Internet and bandwidth** for the electronic part.
3. **Staff need dual skills** (traditional and ICT), requiring constant training.
4. **Duplication** of some resources in both formats, and complex management.

> [!answer]
> Any two: double cost · needs power/Internet for e-resources · staff need traditional and ICT skills · duplication and complex management.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A hybrid library combines the strengths of traditional and digital libraries but also **inherits costs from both sides**: it funds print acquisition and processing _and_ digital subscriptions, ICT and power backup, and it must manage two access systems seamlessly.

## Simplified explanation

Running **two libraries in one** (books and digital) costs more and still needs power and Internet.
hint: A hybrid inherits some weaknesses of both forms.

body: Write short notes on the **two (2) main groups of reference materials** and give **two (2)** examples of **directional tools** in a library. _(Also asked: State five source-type reference materials.)_
answer:
**1. Directional (finding) tools:** point the user to where information can be found, without containing the information itself.
_Examples:_ **bibliographies, indexes, abstracts** (and catalogues).

**2. Source-type materials:** contain the information itself.
_Examples:_ **dictionaries, encyclopaedias, directories, biographical sources, yearbooks/almanacs, atlases/gazetteers, handbooks.**

> [!answer]
> Directional tools (bibliographies, indexes, abstracts) vs source-type materials (dictionaries, encyclopaedias, directories, biographies, yearbooks).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The distinction is about **function**: directional tools are _secondary_ access tools for locating primary literature; source-type materials answer the query directly. A research process often uses both: an index to find articles, an encyclopaedia for background.

## Simplified explanation

Some reference books **show you where to look** (index, bibliography); others **give you the answer** (dictionary, encyclopaedia).
hint: Does it **point to** information or **give** it?

body: Indicate the ways in which information in **reference materials** is arranged.
answer:
1. **Alphabetical**: dictionaries, encyclopaedias
2. **Tabular**: mathematical and statistical works
3. **Regional (geographical)**: maps and atlases
4. **Chronological**: the Bible, history books, timelines
5. **Classified**: by some features or characteristics, as in bibliographies and directories

> [!answer]
> Alphabetical · tabular · regional · chronological · classified.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Reference works are **consulted, not read through**, so their arrangement is chosen to fit the most common way of looking things up: by word (alphabetical), place (regional), time (chronological), subject (classified) or number (tabular).

## Simplified explanation

Dictionary → **A to Z**. Atlas → **by place**. History book → **by date**. Statistics → **tables**. Bibliography → **by subject**.
hint: Think of how a dictionary, an atlas and a history book are each organised.

body: (a) Define a **reference material**. (b) State **four (4)** characteristics of reference materials in libraries.
answer:
**(a)** A reference material is a source **consulted for specific information or facts** rather than read from cover to cover, e.g. a dictionary, encyclopaedia or directory.

**(b) Characteristics:**
1. **Meant to be consulted in the library**: they carry 'Reference Only', 'Not To Be Taken Out' or 'Not To Be Borrowed' labels.
2. **Mostly expensive.**
3. **Not meant to be read from cover to cover.**
4. **Housed in separate sections** of the library, such as the Reference section.
5. **Revised from time to time** to keep abreast of recent developments.
6. **Arranged systematically** (alphabetically, chronologically…) for easy access.

> [!answer]
> Consulted for facts; in-library use only, expensive, not read through, kept in a reference section, revised regularly, systematically arranged.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These characteristics follow from **purpose and value**: because many users need quick access to the same expensive, frequently updated sources, the library keeps them **on site, in one section, systematically arranged**, and replaces them with new editions.

## Simplified explanation

Reference books are **look-up books**. They stay in the library, cost a lot, you do not read them fully, and they get new editions.
hint: Picture the books with 'Reference Only' stickers.

body: (a) What is an **encyclopaedia**? (b) State **four (4)** uses of encyclopaedias.
answer:
**(a)** An encyclopaedia is a book or numbered set of books containing **authoritative summaries of information about a variety of topics** in the form of short essays, usually **arranged alphabetically** by headword or classified in some manner. Example: _New Encyclopaedia Britannica_.

**(b) Uses:**
1. **Finding facts.**
2. **Providing general background** or historical information on a topic.
3. **Serving as guides** to related topics within its pages or to outside sources (cross-references and bibliographies).
4. **Locating explanatory material or definitions.**
5. **Teaching research skills**, i.e. a systematic approach to gathering information.

> [!answer]
> A set of authoritative short-essay summaries on many topics; used for facts, background, guides to further sources, definitions, research skills.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Encyclopaedias are **tertiary sources**: they synthesise knowledge and point onwards through cross-references and bibliographies. Britannica's structure illustrates the uses: **Propaedia** (outline of knowledge), **Micropaedia** (12 vols, ready reference), **Macropaedia** (17 vols, in depth).

## Simplified explanation

An encyclopaedia gives you a **short, trusted summary** of a topic. It is the best **starting point**, and it also points you to more reading.
hint: Where do you start when a topic is new to you?

body: List **two (2)** types of **bibliographies** you know, and state **four (4)** uses of bibliographies.
answer:
**Types:**
1. **Author bibliography**: works by/about one author
2. **Subject bibliography**: works on a subject
3. **National bibliography**: works published in/about a country
4. **Book trade bibliography**: books in print/for sale

**Uses:**
1. **Identify** what has been published on a subject or by an author.
2. **Verify** bibliographic details (author, title, edition, publisher, date) for citation and acquisition.
3. **Locate** sources for research and literature reviews.
4. **Select** materials for acquisition (book trade bibliographies).
5. **Record** a nation's publishing output (national bibliography).

> [!answer]
> Types: author, subject, national, book trade. Uses: identify, verify, locate, select, record publications.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bibliographies are **directional tools**: they list documents with bibliographic details so users can identify, verify and locate them. The **national bibliography**, compiled by the national library from legal-deposit copies, is the backbone of universal bibliographic control.

## Simplified explanation

A bibliography is a **list of books or articles**: by one author, on one subject, from one country, or for sale. It helps you **find and check** sources.
hint: A bibliography is a **list of documents**; ask what such a list helps you do.

body: (a) What is a **periodical**? (b) Give **four (4)** examples of periodicals.
answer:
**(a)** A periodical is a **serial publication with a distinctive title** which appears at **regular or irregular intervals**, generally **more than once a year**, without prior decision as to when the last issue will appear.
_e.g._ _Ghana Library Journal_ 21(2), 2009; _The Mirror_ No. 3058, 17 August 2013.

**(b) Examples:**
1. **Journals**
2. **Magazines**
3. **Newspapers**
4. **Newsletters**
5. **Bulletins**
6. **Reports** (annual)

> [!answer]
> A serial with a distinctive title appearing at intervals, usually more than once a year, with no planned end. Examples: journals, magazines, newspapers, newsletters, bulletins.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Periodicals carry the **most current information**, which is why journals are central to research. Each issue is identified by **volume, issue number and date**, and serials carry an **ISSN** rather than an ISBN.

## Simplified explanation

A periodical **keeps coming out** under the same name (daily, weekly, monthly…) and has no planned last issue: newspapers, magazines, journals.
hint: Key features: one title · repeated issues · no planned last issue.

body: Write short notes on **four (4)** of the following reference materials and indicate their uses: (a) **Encyclopaedias** (b) **Dictionaries** (c) **Indexes** (d) **Directories** (e) **Bibliographies**.
answer:
- **Encyclopaedias:** authoritative summaries of knowledge on many topics as short essays, arranged alphabetically. _Use:_ background, facts, definitions, further references. _e.g._ _Encyclopaedia Britannica_.
- **Dictionaries:** lists of words, usually alphabetical, giving **meaning, spelling, pronunciation, usage and etymology**. Types: general/language, subject (specialised), special (slang, abbreviations, synonyms) and bilingual. _Use:_ meanings and correct usage. _e.g._ _Oxford Dictionary of English_.
- **Indexes:** systematic lists of articles or contents giving **bibliographic details** (author, title, journal, volume, pages) to **locate** items. _Use:_ finding journal articles on a topic.
- **Directories:** lists of **persons or organisations** with **addresses, contacts and other details**. _Use:_ contact and organisational information. _e.g._ telephone directories, university directories.
- **Bibliographies:** lists of documents (books, articles) by an author, on a subject or from a country, with full bibliographic details. _Use:_ identifying and verifying sources.

> [!answer]
> Define each, state its arrangement and use, and give an example.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Group them as **source-type** (encyclopaedias, dictionaries, directories) and **directional** (indexes, bibliographies). Knowing the type of question each answers is the practical skill: _what does it mean?_ → dictionary; _who/where is it?_ → directory; _what has been written on it?_ → bibliography/index; _what is it about?_ → encyclopaedia.

## Simplified explanation

Match the question to the book: **meaning** → dictionary; **overview** → encyclopaedia; **contacts** → directory; **find articles** → index; **list of sources** → bibliography.
hint: Short note = definition + arrangement + use + example.

body: Mention **four (4)** types of **dictionaries** you know.
answer:
1. **General (language) dictionaries**: e.g. _Oxford Dictionary of English_, _Longman Dictionary of Contemporary English_
2. **Subject (specialised) dictionaries**: e.g. _Chambers Dictionary of Science and Technology_, _Dictionary of Information Technology_
3. **Special dictionaries**: one aspect of words (slang, abbreviations, synonyms/antonyms, usage, etymology)
4. **Bilingual/multilingual dictionaries**: e.g. English–French
5. **Biographical/geographical dictionaries**

> [!answer]
> General/language · subject (specialised) · special (one aspect of words) · bilingual.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Dictionaries vary by **scope** (general vs subject), **aspect** (special) and **language** (mono-, bi-, multilingual). Choosing the right type saves time: a technical term is best found in a subject dictionary, slang in a special dictionary.

## Simplified explanation

Some dictionaries cover **all words**, some **one subject**, some **one kind of word** (like slang), and some translate between **two languages**.
hint: Classify by **scope**: all words, one subject, one aspect, two languages.

body: (a) State **five (5)** reference materials found in a **Public Library**. (b) Give **five (5)** reasons why you would recommend a particular reference material to a friend.
answer:
**(a)** Dictionaries · encyclopaedias · directories · yearbooks/almanacs · atlases and gazetteers · biographical sources · handbooks/manuals · bibliographies and indexes.

**(b)** _Recommending an **encyclopaedia** (e.g. Encyclopaedia Britannica):_
1. **Authoritative**: articles written and edited by experts.
2. **Gives background and an overview**, the best starting point on an unfamiliar topic.
3. **Broad coverage** of many subjects in one source.
4. **Easy to use**: alphabetical arrangement, index, cross-references.
5. **Leads to further reading** through bibliographies at the end of articles.
6. **Regularly revised** (new editions/online version), so it stays current.

> [!answer]
> List five reference materials, then justify one (e.g. an encyclopaedia) with five reasons: authority, overview, coverage, ease of use, further references, currency.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Part (b) is an application of **evaluation criteria** (authority, coverage, currency, accessibility) to one reference source. Whatever material you pick, each reason must be **specific to that source** and explained, for 3 marks each.

## Simplified explanation

Name common reference books; then tell your friend why one of them (e.g. an encyclopaedia) is **trustworthy, wide, easy to use and up to date**.
hint: For (b), argue from the source's strengths: authority, coverage, arrangement, currency.

body: (a) What is an **abstract**? (b) Name **two (2)** types of abstracts. (c) Why would a student use an abstract?
answer:
**(a)** An abstract is a **brief summary of the subject content** of a document (article, report, thesis), presented with its **full bibliographic details**.

**(b)**
1. **Informative abstract**: captures all the essential information in the original (purpose, methods, results, conclusions).
2. **Indicative abstract**: shows the principal areas covered and the way the topic has been treated (scope only).

**(c) Why use abstracts:**
1. **Judge relevance quickly** without reading the whole document.
2. **Save time** in literature searches.
3. **Keep up to date** with current research in the field.
4. **Overcome language barriers**: abstracts are often in English even for foreign-language papers.
5. **Decide whether to obtain** the full text (e.g. through ILL/DD).
6. **Support the literature review** by summarising many sources.

> [!answer]
> A brief summary with bibliographic details; informative vs indicative; used to judge relevance, save time, keep current, decide what to read in full.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Abstracts are **secondary sources** compiled by abstracting services (e.g. subject abstracts and databases). An **informative** abstract can stand in for the paper on key findings; an **indicative** one only signals what is covered. A third type, the **critical abstract**, also evaluates the work.

## Simplified explanation

An abstract is a **short summary** of an article. Read it first to see if the article is **worth your time**.
hint: Abstract = index + summary.

body: Explain **four (4)** criteria for evaluating **information sources**.
answer:
1. **Authority:** who created it, and what are their credentials, expertise and affiliation?
2. **Accuracy:** is the information correct, verifiable and supported by evidence or references?
3. **Objectivity:** is it balanced and free from bias, or written to sell or persuade?
4. **Currency:** when was it published or last updated, and is it recent enough for the topic?
5. **Coverage/relevance:** does it cover the topic in the depth you need and suit your purpose?

> [!answer]
> Authority · accuracy · objectivity · currency · coverage/relevance, each explained.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These criteria operationalise **ACRL Standard 3** (evaluate information critically). They apply to any format, but they matter most online, where there is no editorial or central control. Some courses package them as the **CRAAP test**: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

## Simplified explanation

Ask **who** wrote it, **is it true**, **is it fair**, **is it recent**, and **is it what I need**.
hint: The same criteria apply to print and web sources.

body: What are the **two (2)** major ways of citing (acknowledging) your sources **within a text**? Illustrate each with an example. _(Also asked: list two forms of citation you know.)_
answer:
**1. Author-prominent (narrative) citation:** the author's name is part of the sentence, followed by the year (and page for quotations) in brackets.
- _Research by **Alemna and Badu (2005)** showed that…_
- _According to **Dhoti (1998)**, "Students often had difficulty using APA style when it was their first time" (p. 199)._

**2. Information-prominent (parenthetical) citation:** the information comes first; author and year go in brackets at the end.
- _Students often struggle with APA style the first time they use it **(Dhoti, 1998, p. 199)**._
- _Information literacy improves academic performance **(Alemna & Badu, 2005)**._

> [!answer]
> Narrative (author-prominent): Mensah (2020) states… · Parenthetical (information-prominent): …(Mensah, 2020).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In APA, use **'and'** inside running text but **`&`** inside brackets: _Alemna and Badu (2005)_ vs _(Alemna & Badu, 2005)_. Direct quotations need a **page number** (`p. 199`). With three or more authors, APA 7 uses `et al.` from the first citation, e.g. `(Yawson et al., 2026)`. Every in-text citation must match an entry in the **reference list**.

## Simplified explanation

Either **name the author in your sentence** (_Mensah (2020) says…_) or **put the name in brackets at the end** (_…(Mensah, 2020)_).
hint: Is the author's name inside the sentence or in the brackets?

body: Mention **in full** the two (2) major citation styles you were taught and the **disciplines** associated with them. _(Also asked: mention any four (4) citation styles you have studied.)_
answer:
| Style | In full | Disciplines |
|---|---|---|
| **APA** | **American Psychological Association** | Social sciences: psychology, education, business, sociology |
| **MLA** | **Modern Language Association** | Humanities, especially languages and literature |

_Other styles:_ **Chicago** (history, some humanities) · **Harvard** (author–date, many disciplines) · **IEEE** (engineering, computing) · **Vancouver** (medicine, health sciences) · **AMA** (medicine) · **ASA** (sociology).

> [!answer]
> APA = American Psychological Association (social sciences); MLA = Modern Language Association (humanities: languages & literature).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Disciplines adopt styles that suit their writing. **APA** is author–**date** because social science values recency of research. **MLA** is author–**page** because literary work quotes texts closely. UCC uses **APA** institutionally.

## Simplified explanation

**APA** for social sciences, **MLA** for languages and literature. Spell them out fully.
hint: Write the names **in full**: abbreviations alone lose marks.

body: State any **three (3)** marked differences in **out-text referencing** (reference list) between the **APA** and **MLA** citation styles.
answer:
| Feature | APA | MLA |
|---|---|---|
| **Title of the list** | _References_ | _Works Cited_ |
| **Author names** | Surname + **initials** (Mensah, K. A.) | Surname + **full first name** (Mensah, Kofi A.) |
| **Position of date** | **Right after the author(s)**, in brackets: (2015). | **Near the end**, after the publisher, no brackets: …, 2015. |
| **Title capitalisation** | **Sentence case** | **Title Case** |
| **Article titles** | Plain, no quotation marks | In **"quotation marks"** |
| **Joining authors** | `&` | `and` |

> [!answer]
> Any three: References vs Works Cited · initials vs full first names · date after author vs at the end · sentence case vs title case · article titles plain vs in quotes · & vs and.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The differences come from the styles' priorities: **APA (author–date)** puts the year up front because recency matters in the social sciences; **MLA (author–page)** foregrounds full names and titles, valued in the humanities.

## Simplified explanation

APA: _Mensah, K. (2015). Title in sentence case._ MLA: _Mensah, Kofi. Title in Title Case. 2015._ Notice the **names**, the **date position** and the **capitals**.
hint: Compare where the **date** goes and how **names** are written.

body: Using the **APA** citation style, write a reference for the following: The title of the book is _"Introduction to Educational Psychology"_, written by **Arnold K. Nayak** and **Victor K. Rao**, and published in **2004** by **A.P.H. Publishing Corporation**, in **New Delhi**.
answer:
**Reference:**

> [!answer]
> Nayak, A. K., & Rao, V. K. (2004). _Introduction to educational psychology_. New Delhi: A.P.H. Publishing Corporation.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**APA book pattern:** `Surname, Initials., & Surname, Initials. (Year). Title in sentence case (ed.). Place: Publisher.`
- Surname first, then **initials**; join the last two authors with **`&`**.
- **Year** in brackets right after the authors.
- Title in _italics_ and **sentence case** (capitalise only the first word, the first word after a colon, and proper nouns).
- Edition in brackets after the title, e.g. `(5th ed.)`. Omit it for a first edition.
- `Place: Publisher.` (APA 6, as taught in ILT 101). **APA 7 drops the place.**

First edition, so no edition statement. The title becomes **sentence case**: _Introduction to educational psychology_.

**APA 7 version** (no place of publication):

> Nayak, A. K., & Rao, V. K. (2004). _Introduction to educational psychology_. A.P.H. Publishing Corporation.

## Simplified explanation

Write the **surnames first**, then the initials: _Nayak, A. K., & Rao, V. K._ Then the year, the title in italics with only the first word capitalised, then _place: publisher_.

> [!warning]
> Common mark-losers: full first names instead of **initials**, missing `&`, Title Case instead of **sentence case**, title not _italicised_, edition in the wrong place.
hint: Author(s) → (Year) → _Title_ → (edition) → Place: Publisher.

body: Three (3) University professors **Kwesi Atta Bosomafie**, **Kweku Tawiah Gyankabo** and **Adjoa Monkah Odasanyi** _edited_ the **fifth edition** of a book titled _The erstwhile Savage: memoirs of a disillusioned Gold Coaster_. The book was published in **2010** by **Asempa Publications** in **Cape Coast**. Use the **APA** citation style to write a reference for the book.
answer:
**Reference:**

> [!answer]
> Bosomafie, K. A., Gyankabo, K. T., & Odasanyi, A. M. (Eds.). (2010). _The erstwhile savage: Memoirs of a disillusioned Gold Coaster_ (5th ed.). Cape Coast: Asempa Publications.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**APA book pattern:** `Surname, Initials., & Surname, Initials. (Year). Title in sentence case (ed.). Place: Publisher.`
- Surname first, then **initials**; join the last two authors with **`&`**.
- **Year** in brackets right after the authors.
- Title in _italics_ and **sentence case** (capitalise only the first word, the first word after a colon, and proper nouns).
- Edition in brackets after the title, e.g. `(5th ed.)`. Omit it for a first edition.
- `Place: Publisher.` (APA 6, as taught in ILT 101). **APA 7 drops the place.**

The people are **editors**, so add **`(Eds.)`** after the names. Capitalise the first word after the colon (_Memoirs_) and the proper noun _Gold Coaster_.

**APA 7 version** (no place of publication):

> Bosomafie, K. A., Gyankabo, K. T., & Odasanyi, A. M. (Eds.). (2010). _The erstwhile savage: Memoirs of a disillusioned Gold Coaster_ (5th ed.). Asempa Publications.

## Simplified explanation

Because they **edited** the book, put _(Eds.)_ after their names. Then year, title in italics, _(5th ed.)_, place and publisher.

> [!warning]
> Common mark-losers: full first names instead of **initials**, missing `&`, Title Case instead of **sentence case**, title not _italicised_, edition in the wrong place.
hint: Edited book: names → (Eds.) → (Year) → _Title_ → (5th ed.) → Place: Publisher.

body: In the year **2015**, **University of Cape Coast Press** published the **seventh edition** of **Dr. Koffi Manu** and **Mrs. Abena Morrison**'s book entitled _"The fishmonger's adventure at Duakor."_ Using the **APA** citation style, write a reference for the above bibliographic information.
answer:
**Reference:**

> [!answer]
> Manu, K., & Morrison, A. (2015). _The fishmonger's adventure at Duakor_ (7th ed.). Cape Coast: University of Cape Coast Press.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**APA book pattern:** `Surname, Initials., & Surname, Initials. (Year). Title in sentence case (ed.). Place: Publisher.`
- Surname first, then **initials**; join the last two authors with **`&`**.
- **Year** in brackets right after the authors.
- Title in _italics_ and **sentence case** (capitalise only the first word, the first word after a colon, and proper nouns).
