body: Define **copyright** and state **three (3)** 'exclusive rights' the creator of an original work enjoys under the copyright law. _(Also asked: define exclusive rights.)_
answer:
**Copyright** is a legal term/concept that gives the **creator of an original work exclusive rights** to control the use of their work **for a limited time**. (WIPO: the rights given to creators for their literary and artistic works.)

**Exclusive rights** are the rights reserved **solely** for the copyright owner:
1. **The right to make copies** (reproduce the work).
2. **The right to be credited** for the work (attribution).
3. **The right to determine who may adapt the work** into derivative forms (translations, performances) and to **benefit financially** from the work, plus other related rights (distribution, public performance/display).

> [!answer]
> Copyright = exclusive rights of a creator to control their original work for a limited time. Rights: copy · be credited · authorise adaptations/derivatives and benefit financially.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In Ghana copyright is governed by the **Copyright Act, 2005 (Act 690)**, after the Copyright Act 85 of 1961 and PNDC Law 110. Copyright **gives creators a monopoly to stimulate creativity**; creators may **transfer** those rights to publishers; and **users have fair-use rights**. Exclusive rights are economic (copy, distribute, adapt, perform) and moral (attribution, integrity).

## Simplified explanation

Copyright is the **law that says your work belongs to you**. Only you can copy it, adapt it and earn from it, and you must be credited.
hint: Exclusive = only the creator may do (or permit) it.

body: For how long will a creator of a work enjoy the 'exclusive rights' under the copyright law in **Ghana**?
answer:
1. **Single author:** during the **life of the author and seventy (70) years after the death** of the author.
2. **Co-authored work:** during the life of the **last surviving author** and **seventy (70) years after** that author's death.

> [!answer]
> Life of the author + 70 years (for joint works, 70 years after the death of the last surviving author).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

This comes from the **Copyright Act, 2005 (Act 690)**, in line with international norms (Berne Convention minimum of life + 50; many countries now life + 70). After the term expires the work enters the **public domain** and may be used freely.

## Simplified explanation

Your work is protected **all your life and 70 years after you die**.
hint: Life + ?

body: For a work to be granted **copyright protection**, it must meet certain criteria. State **two (2)** of such criteria.
answer:
1. **Fixation:** the work must be **fixed in a definite medium of expression** (written, recorded, saved), not just an idea in the head.
2. **Originality:** the work must be **original**, the result of the author's/creator's own **skill and effort**.
3. **Nationality/place of publication:** the creator must be a **citizen** of the country, or the work must have been **first published in the country** before anywhere else.

> [!answer]
> Fixed in a definite medium · original (author's own skill and effort) · author a citizen or work first published in the country.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Copyright protects the **expression**, not the idea. Fixation provides evidence of the expression; originality requires independent creation with a minimum of skill; the nationality/first-publication rule decides which country's law applies.

## Simplified explanation

Your work must be **written down or recorded**, be **your own original work**, and be **by a citizen or first published here**.
hint: Ideas alone are not protected. What else is needed?

body: State the **legal exceptions** to the copyright law. _(Also asked: provide two conditions under which the exclusive rights of copyright laws are not applicable.)_
answer:
1. **Fair use (fair dealing):** users may use limited parts of a work without permission for **private study, research, criticism, review, news reporting and teaching**, with acknowledgement.
2. **Transfer of rights:** authors/creators may **transfer their monopolistic rights to publishers** for marketing purposes, so the publisher, not the author, exercises them.
3. **Expiry of the term:** after life + 70 years the work enters the **public domain**.
4. **Library and archival use:** limited reproduction for preservation or replacement.

> [!answer]
> Fair use (study, research, criticism, teaching, news) · transfer of rights to publishers · expiry into the public domain · limited library copying.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The 'main issues' in copyright law as taught: it **gives monopoly** to creators to stimulate creativity; creators **may transfer** these rights to publishers; and **users have rights in the form of fair use**. Exceptions balance the private incentive to create with the public interest in access to knowledge.

## Simplified explanation

You may use small parts of a work **for study, research or teaching** with credit (fair use), and works become **free to use** once copyright expires.
hint: When can someone use a work without the author's permission?

body: (a) What is **plagiarism**? (b) Outline **three (3)** ways of avoiding plagiarism. (c) State **two (2)** consequences (penalties) of plagiarism.
answer:
**(a)** Plagiarism means **claiming or implying original authorship** of someone else's written or creative work, in whole or in part, **without adequate acknowledgement**. It is academic theft or fraud.

**(b) Avoiding plagiarism:**
1. **Clearly acknowledge** the source of any borrowed words or ideas (in-text citation + reference list).
2. **Paraphrase properly**: restate ideas in your own words and structure, **and still cite**.
3. **Use quotation marks** for words copied exactly, with page numbers.
4. **Take careful notes** recording the source details of everything you read.
5. **Use plagiarism-checking software** (e.g. Turnitin) before submitting.

**(c) Consequences:**
1. **Failing** the assignment or course, or loss of marks.
2. **Suspension or dismissal** from the university.
3. **Withdrawal of a degree** already awarded.
4. **Legal action** for copyright infringement, fines.
5. **Loss of reputation and credibility.**

> [!answer]
> Using another's work as your own without acknowledgement; avoid by citing, paraphrasing with citation, quoting, careful notes; penalties: failure, suspension/dismissal, degree withdrawal, legal action, lost reputation.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Plagiarism breaches **ACRL Standard 5** (ethical/legal use of information) and the university's academic integrity rules. **Paraphrasing without citation is still plagiarism.** The fix is attribution, not rewording. Self-plagiarism (re-submitting your own earlier work) is also an offence.

## Simplified explanation

Plagiarism is **using someone else's work as if it were yours**. Always **say where you got it**, or you can fail or even be sacked.

> [!warning]
> Changing a few words does **not** make it your work. You must still cite.
hint: Plagiarism is about **acknowledgement**, not about whether the words are changed.

body: Give **three (3)** specific examples of acts that constitute **plagiarism**.
answer:
1. **Copying text** from the Internet, a book or an article **without citing** the source and claiming ownership.
2. **Rewriting (paraphrasing) a text in your own words without stating** the source.
3. **Paying for an essay** (or getting someone to write it) and presenting it as your own.
4. **Handing in another student's work** under your own name.
5. **Copying statistics, maps, tables or charts** without stating the source.

> [!answer]
> Copying without citation · paraphrasing without citation · buying/ghost-written essays · submitting another student's work · copying data, tables or charts without source.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Each example fails the same test: **the reader cannot tell which work is not yours**. Plagiarism covers **words, ideas, data and media**, whether intentional or careless.

## Simplified explanation

Any time you hand in **someone else's words, ideas, essay or charts** without saying whose they are, it is plagiarism.
hint: Think of words, ideas, whole papers and data.

body: Briefly explain any three (3) of the following terms: (i) **Copyright** (ii) **Cataloguing** (iii) **Plagiarism** (iv) **Classification** (v) **Corporate authorship**.
answer:
- **Copyright:** a legal concept giving the creator of an original work **exclusive rights** to control its use for a limited time (in Ghana, life + 70 years).
- **Cataloguing:** the **process of recording information about an item** according to accepted standards (author, title, edition, publisher, year…) to produce catalogue entries.
- **Plagiarism:** claiming or implying authorship of someone else's work, in whole or in part, **without adequate acknowledgement**.
- **Classification:** the **process of grouping**: putting like entities together and separating unlike ones. In libraries, books are arranged on the shelves by subject using a scheme (DDC or LC). _Sayers (1975): the arrangement of books on the shelves, or descriptions of them, in the manner most useful to those who read._
- **Corporate authorship:** when an **organisation** (government ministry, university, company, association) **rather than an individual** is responsible for a work, the body is treated as the author, e.g. _University of Cape Coast. (2020). Annual report._

> [!answer]
> Copyright = exclusive rights; cataloguing = describing items; plagiarism = unacknowledged use; classification = grouping by subject; corporate author = organisation as author.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cataloguing and classification are the two **tools for organising knowledge**: cataloguing **describes** items (what is it?) and classification **places** them by subject (where is it?). Copyright and plagiarism are both **ethical/legal** issues: one is a law protecting creators; the other is an academic offence of non-attribution.

## Simplified explanation

**Cataloguing** describes a book; **classification** shelves it by subject; **copyright** protects the author; **plagiarism** steals credit; a **corporate author** is an organisation.
hint: One or two precise sentences per term.

body: '_Cataloguing is a process and a Catalogue is a product._' Explain this statement in your own words. _(Also asked: What is a library catalogue?)_
answer:
- **Cataloguing (the process):** the activity of **recording information about each item** according to accepted standards: author, title, edition, publisher, year, pages, subject, call number.
- **Catalogue (the product):** the **result**: a **list of the documents in a library**, with entries arranged in a systematic order, that shows **what the library has and where each item can be found**.

So cataloguing is **what librarians do**; the catalogue is **what users consult**.

> [!answer]
> Cataloguing is the act of describing items to standard; the catalogue is the resulting systematic list showing what the library holds and where.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The process applies standards (AACR2/RDA, MARC) so records are consistent and exchangeable; the product may take several **forms** (card, book, sheaf, microform, OPAC). Good cataloguing determines the quality of **access points** in the product.

## Simplified explanation

Cataloguing is like **writing the list**; the catalogue is **the finished list** you search.
hint: Process = doing; product = result.

body: State **three (3)** reasons why library materials are **catalogued** (organised).
answer:
1. **To enable a user to find a book** whose **author, title or subject** is known.
2. **To show what the library has** by a given author, on a given subject and in a given kind of literature.
3. **To assist users in the choice of a book** as to its **edition** or its **character** (topical, literary).
4. **Easy retrieval** of materials and saving users' time.

> [!answer]
> To find a known item (author/title/subject) · to show what the library holds · to help choose an edition or kind of book · easy retrieval.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These are **Charles Cutter's (1876) objects of the catalogue**: _finding_ (a known item), _collocating_ (showing all works of an author or subject together) and _choice_ (selecting by edition or character). They still underpin modern cataloguing models (FRBR: find, identify, select, obtain).

## Simplified explanation

We catalogue so you can **find** a book, **see** everything on a topic or by an author, and **choose** the right edition.
hint: Cutter's objects of the catalogue: find, collocate, choose.

body: Mention **four (4)** library **access points**. _(Also asked: means by which a library's catalogue can be accessed.)_
answer:
**Access points**, the codes or terms used to locate a record in a catalogue or database:
1. **Call mark/call number**
2. **Author**
3. **Title**
4. **Subject**
5. **Series**
6. **ISBN/ISSN**

> [!answer]
> Call mark · author · title · subject · series · ISBN.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Access points are the **headings** under which records are filed or indexed. A good record provides several, so a user who knows only part of the information (just a subject, or an ISBN) can still find the item.

## Simplified explanation

You can find a book by its **author, title, subject, call number, series or ISBN**.
hint: What can you type or look up to find a book?

body: State the primary **forms of library catalogues** and explain any **two (2)** of them.
answer:
**Forms:** **card**, **book (printed)**, **sheaf**, **microform** and **computer/online (OPAC)** catalogues.

- **Card catalogue:** each entry is typed on a standard card (`7.5 × 12.5 cm`) filed in drawers in a cabinet, by author, title or subject. _Easy to update_ but bulky and usable only on site.
- **Book (printed) catalogue:** entries printed in book form. _Portable and can be distributed_, but quickly out of date.
- **Sheaf catalogue:** entries on slips held in loose-leaf binders. _Flexible and compact_ but slips can be lost.
- **Microform catalogue:** entries on microfilm/microfiche, read with a reader. _Compact_ but needs equipment.
- **OPAC (Online Public Access Catalogue):** a computerised catalogue searched by terminal or over the Internet. _Remote access, many access points, keyword and Boolean search, shows availability._

> [!answer]
> Card, book, sheaf, microform, OPAC. Explain two with features and pros/cons.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The forms reflect technology over time. Modern libraries use the **OPAC**, based on **MARC** records, often integrated into a library management system and discovery layer, though some keep the card catalogue for older materials.

## Simplified explanation

A catalogue can be **cards in drawers**, a **printed book**, **loose slips**, **microfilm**, or a **computer search (OPAC)**.
hint: Five physical forms, from cards in drawers to online.

body: State any **two (2)** advantages the **Online Public Access Catalogue (OPAC)** has over the **Card Catalogue**.
answer:
1. **Remote access:** searchable from anywhere via the Internet, any time.
2. **More access points and keyword/Boolean searching**, not just author, title and subject.
3. **Shows real-time availability** (on loan, due date, location).
4. **Multiple users** can search at the same time.
5. **Easier and faster to update**, and saves space.

> [!answer]
> Any two: remote 24/7 access · keyword/Boolean search on many fields · live availability status · simultaneous users · easy updating and no bulky cabinets.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The OPAC is part of an integrated library system: catalogue records (MARC) link to **circulation**, so status is live. It supports field and keyword searching, limits and links to e-resources: the access and evaluation skills of ACRL Standard 2.

## Simplified explanation

OPAC lets you search **from your phone, any time**, by any word, and see if the book is **on the shelf**.
hint: What can a computer do that a drawer of cards cannot?

body: Identify the **two (2)** major **classification schemes** and indicate the type of library that uses each.
answer:
1. **Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC):** numbers `000–999` divided decimally (e.g. `020` Library science). Commonly used in **public and school** libraries.
2. **Library of Congress Classification (LC):** letters plus numbers (e.g. `Z` Bibliography and library science, `QA76` Computers). Commonly used in **academic and research** libraries (e.g. UCC).

> [!answer]
> DDC (public & school libraries) and LC (academic & research libraries).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

DDC divides knowledge into **10 main classes** by number, which suits general collections. LC's **21 lettered classes** (A–Z, omitting I, O, W, X, Y) expand easily for very large scholarly collections, hence its use in universities.

## Simplified explanation

**Dewey** (numbers) for public and school libraries; **Library of Congress** (letters) for university libraries.
hint: One uses numbers, the other letters.

body: Provide the corresponding **discipline** of the following **Library of Congress** classes: **D**, **J**, **N**, **R**, **S**, **T**.
answer:
| Class | Discipline |
|---|---|
| **D** | History (General) and History of the Old World |
| **J** | Political Science |
| **N** | Fine Arts |
| **R** | Medicine |
| **S** | Agriculture |
| **T** | Technology |

> [!answer]
> D History · J Political science · N Fine arts · R Medicine · S Agriculture · T Technology.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**LC main classes:** A General works · B Philosophy, Psychology, Religion · C Auxiliary sciences of history · D World history · E–F History of the Americas · G Geography, Anthropology, Recreation · H Social sciences · J Political science · K Law · L Education · M Music · N Fine arts · P Language & literature · Q Science · R Medicine · S Agriculture · T Technology · U Military science · V Naval science · Z Bibliography & library science.

## Simplified explanation

Memorise the letters: **J**=politics, **N**=art, **R**=medicine, **S**=agriculture, **T**=technology, **D**=history.

> [!tip]
> Tricky ones: **J** (not 'journalism') = Political science; **K** = Law; **Z** = Library science.
hint: Learn the LC outline as a table.

body: Distinguish clearly between **INFORMATION** and **KNOWLEDGE** as terms in Information Literacy.
answer:
- **Information:** **facts or data** that have been **collected, recorded, processed and stored** in a retrievable form, e.g. the statistics in a report.
- **Knowledge:** **human inferences and interpretation derived from processed information**, i.e. the understanding a person builds by applying, relating and reflecting on information, e.g. a researcher's conclusion from the statistics.

| | Information | Knowledge |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Processed data | Interpreted, internalised information |
| Location | Stored in documents, databases | In people's minds (and expressed in work) |
| Transfer | Easily copied and shared | Built through learning and experience |

> [!answer]
> Information = processed, recorded data; knowledge = human interpretation and understanding derived from information.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Think of the DIKW hierarchy: **data → information → knowledge → wisdom**. Libraries organise **recorded information**; information literacy is the bridge by which individuals turn it into **knowledge**, through evaluation and use.

## Simplified explanation

**Information** is the facts in the book; **knowledge** is what you understand after reading and thinking about them.
hint: Which one lives in a database and which lives in your head?

body: What do these abbreviations stand for? (a) **ISBN** (b) **ISSN**.
answer:
- **ISBN:** International Standard Book Number, the unique identifier for a **book** (edition-specific; 13 digits since 2007).
- **ISSN:** International Standard Serial Number, the unique 8-digit identifier for a **serial/periodical** (journal, magazine, newspaper).

> [!answer]
> ISBN = International Standard Book Number; ISSN = International Standard Serial Number.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Both are assigned by **national agencies** (in Ghana via the national library) as part of bibliographic control, and both serve as **access points** in catalogues and in book-trade systems.

## Simplified explanation

**ISBN** is a book's ID number; **ISSN** is a journal's or magazine's ID number.
hint: Book vs serial.

body:
The main library of the University of Cape Coast recently acquired the following item. As a **cataloguer**, process it for easy retrieval:

The material has **more than three authors**, namely Christian Kofi, Wilfred Biney, William Baiden and Korklu Laryea. It has **twenty-four preliminary pages**, **six hundred and fifteen textual pages** with **illustrations**. The title is _Reporting technical information_, **fifth edition**. The **call mark** is `T11 .R29` and the **accession number** is `226452`. The **ISBN** is `0-19-517879-3`, and it **includes bibliography and subject index**.
answer:
**Main entry under TITLE** (four authors, more than three, so no author main entry):

```
T11       Reporting technical information / Christian Kofi … [et al.].
.R29      — 5th ed. — xxiv, 615 p. : ill.
          Includes bibliography and index.
          ISBN 0-19-517879-3

          1. Technical writing.  I. Kofi, Christian.

226452
```

- **Call mark** `T11 .R29` at top left (T = Technology).
- **Title main entry**, with statement of responsibility naming the **first author + [et al.]**.
- **Edition** `5th ed.`, **collation** `xxiv, 615 p. : ill.`, **notes**, **ISBN**.
- **Tracings:** subject heading and added entry for the first author.
- **Accession number** `226452` at the bottom.

> [!answer]
> Title main entry (more than three authors), with call mark, title / first author [et al.], 5th ed., xxiv, 615 p. : ill., notes, ISBN, tracings, accession number.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Under **AACR2 rule 21.6C2**, a work by **more than three** authors gets its **main entry under title**, with an added entry for the **first-named author**. Preliminary pages are given in **lower-case Roman numerals** (`xxiv`) and text pages in Arabic numerals (`615 p.`), with `ill.` for illustrations. The place, publisher and date were not supplied, so they are left out (or `[S.l. : s.n.]`).

## Simplified explanation

Because there are **four** authors, the card starts with the **title**. Then add the edition, pages (xxiv, 615 p.), ill., notes, ISBN, and put the call mark at the top and the accession number at the bottom.
hint: Rule of three: with **more than three** authors the entry goes under **title**.

body: Arrange the following authors in **alphabetical order** (as in a catalogue): (i) Kwame Boohene (ii) Kobina Boohene (iii) Kwame Boohene (iv) Kwabena Boohene.
answer:
1. **Boohene, Kobina** _(ii)_
2. **Boohene, Kwabena** _(iv)_
3. **Boohene, Kwame** _(i)_
4. **Boohene, Kwame** _(iii)_

> [!answer]
> Boohene, Kobina → Boohene, Kwabena → Boohene, Kwame → Boohene, Kwame.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Personal names are filed **surname first**; with identical surnames, filing moves to the forenames letter by letter: K-**o**-bina before K-**w**-abena (o < w); Kw-a-**b**-ena before Kw-a-**m**-e (b < m). Identical headings (the two Kwame Boohenes) file together, then by title or date.

## Simplified explanation

Write **surname first**. All are Boohene, so compare first names: **Ko**bina, **Kwab**ena, **Kwam**e, **Kwam**e.
hint: Same surname, so sort by the first name letter by letter.

body: Explain what the **Internet** is.
answer:
The Internet is a **global network of computer networks**: a large computer network connecting a vast number of computers all around the world, linking millions of businesses, government agencies, educational institutions and individuals. The computers communicate using common **protocols (TCP/IP)**. The Internet is **not centrally controlled**: the owners of its various parts maintain them.

> [!answer]
> A decentralised, global network of computer networks communicating by TCP/IP.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The Internet is the **infrastructure**; the **World Wide Web** is one service running on it (hyperlinked pages accessed by browsers over HTTP), alongside email, file transfer and VoIP. Its decentralisation is why the reliability of online information must be **evaluated** by the user.

## Simplified explanation

The Internet links **computers all over the world** so they can share information. **No one person or government** controls it.
hint: Three ideas: global · network of networks · no central control.

body: Searching on the Internet can sometimes be an overwhelming task. State (and explain) the **basic steps** one can employ to effectively retrieve information from the Internet, **in the right order**.
answer:
1. **Define your information need**: what exactly you want (a specific fact, or general background?), how much, at what depth, and for whom.
2. **Choose your search terms**: identify unique keywords and key phrases, and consider synonyms, alternative spellings, plurals and acronyms.
3. **Decide which sources/search tool to use**: a search engine, metasearch engine, subject directory or academic database, depending on the need.
4. **Find out how the search tool functions**: its search syntax: Boolean operators, phrase searching (`" "`), truncation (`*`), field limits, advanced search.
5. **Run your search**: enter the query combining terms with the right operators.
6. **Review and refine (revise) your search**: assess results for relevance; narrow (AND, more specific terms) or broaden (OR, synonyms, truncation) and repeat.

> [!answer]
> Define the need → choose search terms → decide the search tool → learn how the tool works → run the search → review and refine.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

This is a **search strategy**: a planned, iterative process instead of trial-and-error typing. Steps 1–3 are conceptual (and can be done offline); steps 4–6 apply the tool's syntax. Refinement uses **Boolean logic** and **truncation/phrase** techniques. The strategy saves time and bandwidth and improves **precision** (relevant hits) and **recall** (coverage).

## Simplified explanation

Know **what** you want, pick **keywords**, choose **where** to search, learn **how** that tool works, **search**, then **check and improve** your results.

> [!tip]
> Order matters: write the steps **numbered and in sequence**.
hint: Six steps; the first three can be done away from the computer.

body: Give **three (3)** reasons why one must search effectively on the Internet.
answer:
1. **There are huge amounts of resources online** (information overload); without a strategy you drown in irrelevant results.
2. **The World Wide Web is not indexed or catalogued** as a whole, so careful searches are needed to find relevant, quality material.
3. **For effective use of resources** such as **bandwidth, money, time and computers**.
4. **Much online information is unreliable**, so targeted searching of quality tools (academic databases) yields credible sources.

> [!answer]
> Information overload · the Web is not catalogued · saving bandwidth, money, time and computers · quality of information varies.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Unlike a library collection, the Web has **no selection, no cataloguing and no central control**. Effective searching (keywords, Boolean logic, the right tools) compensates by raising **precision** and saving scarce resources such as data bundles and time.

## Simplified explanation

The Internet is **huge and messy**, and data and time cost money, so you must **search smartly**.
hint: Think of the cost of aimless searching.

body: State and explain **three (3)** common uses of the Internet. _(Also asked: two uses of the Internet to society.)_
answer:
1. **Communication:** email, instant messaging, VoIP, social networking, audio and video conferencing, all instant and cheap across distances.
2. **Education and research:** access to e-journals, academic databases, e-books, online courses (MOOCs) and e-learning platforms.
3. **Entertainment:** music, videos, games, streaming and social media.
4. **Online services:** e-banking, e-government (online registration and payments), booking and ticketing.
5. **E-commerce:** buying and selling goods and services online (Jumia, mobile money payments).
6. **Information dissemination:** news, announcements and public information.

> [!answer]
> Any three, each explained: communication · education & research · entertainment · online services · e-commerce · information dissemination.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These uses show the Internet as a **platform**: the same TCP/IP infrastructure supports communication, publication, commerce and services. For students, **education and research** is central: subscribed databases and open-access repositories give access to scholarly literature far beyond the physical library.

## Simplified explanation

People use the Internet to **talk to others**, **learn and research**, **have fun**, **bank and pay bills**, and **buy things**.
hint: State **and** explain, with examples, for 3 marks each.

body: Explain **four (4)** **academic benefits** of the Internet.
answer:
1. **Access to scholarly resources:** e-journals, academic databases (JSTOR, SAGE, AGORA), e-books and institutional repositories, any time.
2. **E-learning and distance education:** LMS platforms (e.g. Moodle), MOOCs and online lectures support flexible learning, as at CoDE.
3. **Collaboration and communication:** email, discussion forums and video conferencing with lecturers and peers across the world.
4. **Up-to-date information:** current research, news and data faster than print.
5. **Research tools:** citation managers, online surveys, plagiarism checkers and data sources.

> [!answer]
> Access to scholarly e-resources · e-learning/distance education · academic collaboration · current information · research tools.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The academic value of the Internet depends on **information literacy**: the same channel that gives access to peer-reviewed literature also carries misinformation, so the benefits are realised through skilled searching (search strategy) and critical **evaluation**.

## Simplified explanation

The Internet lets students **read journals online, take online classes, work with others far away, and get the latest information**.
hint: Focus on learning and research only.

body: Explain **four (4)** misuses (disadvantages) of the Internet. _(Also asked: list three uses and three misuses; outline three disadvantages of using the Internet.)_
answer:
1. **Identity theft/fraud:** stealing personal information (passwords, bank details) to impersonate victims, e.g. through **phishing** emails that appear to come from a bank.
2. **Spamming:** sending unsolicited, unwanted bulk messages, wasting time and storage and often carrying scams.
3. **Pornography:** easy access to obscene materials, especially harmful to minors.
4. **Computer virus threats:** malicious code spread through downloads and attachments that disrupts computers and destroys data.
5. **Cyberbullying and misinformation (fake news).**
6. **Plagiarism and copyright infringement** made easy by copy-and-paste.

> [!answer]
> Identity theft/fraud (phishing) · spamming · pornography · computer viruses · cyberbullying · misinformation · plagiarism.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These misuses come from the same openness and anonymity that make the Internet powerful. Protection combines **technology** (antivirus, spam filters, strong passwords, two-factor authentication), **law** (e.g. Ghana's Cybersecurity Act 2020) and **user literacy** (recognising phishing, evaluating sources).

## Simplified explanation

Bad uses of the Internet: **stealing people's identities, junk messages, pornography, viruses, bullying and fake news**.
hint: The notes' four: identity theft, spamming, pornography, virus threat.

body: Briefly explain the following, identified as disadvantages of using the Internet: (i) **Spamming** (ii) **Computer virus** (iii) **Identity theft/fraud**.
answer:
- **Spamming:** sending **unsolicited and unwanted bulk messages** (email, SMS, social media), usually adverts or scams. It clogs inboxes and wastes time and bandwidth.
- **Computer virus:** a **program or code that disrupts the normal functioning** of a computer when loaded onto it; it replicates and spreads through files, downloads and email attachments, corrupting or deleting data.
- **Identity theft/fraud:** **stealing someone's personal information** (names, passwords, card or bank details) to impersonate them for financial gain, often via **phishing**: emails or websites that appear to come from legitimate sources such as a bank.

> [!answer]
> Spam = unsolicited bulk messages; virus = code disrupting computers; identity theft = stealing personal data to impersonate victims (e.g. phishing).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

All three are **cyber-threats** with different targets: spam targets **attention and resources**, viruses target **systems and data**, identity theft targets **people and money**. They often combine: spam carries phishing links or virus attachments.

## Simplified explanation

**Spam** = junk messages. **Virus** = a harmful program that breaks your computer. **Identity theft** = someone stealing your details to pretend to be you.
hint: Definition + effect for each.

body: Write short notes on a **(web) browser** and give **examples**. _(Also asked: What is a browser? Briefly describe a browser and give two examples.)_
answer:
A **web browser** is **software (a program) used to navigate or access the Internet**, displaying web pages and retrieving files. Browsers can also be used for communication and for accessing information on web servers in private networks or files in file systems. **Without a browser, one cannot access the Web.**

**Types and examples:**
- **Graphic-based browsers**: render text, images, audio and video: **Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge (formerly Internet Explorer), Safari, Opera**; historically Netscape Navigator.
- **Text-based browsers**: display only text: **Lynx**; historically Mosaic.

> [!answer]
> Software for accessing and navigating the Web; graphic-based (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari) and text-based (Lynx).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A browser is a **client** application: it requests resources by **URL** using **HTTP/HTTPS**, then interprets HTML, CSS and JavaScript to render pages. Don't confuse a **browser** (Chrome) with a **search engine** (Google Search), which is a website you open **in** a browser.

## Simplified explanation

A browser is the **app you use to open websites**, like Chrome or Firefox.

> [!warning]
> **Google** is a search engine; **Google Chrome** is a browser.
hint: Define it, say what it does, then two types with examples.

body: List **four (4)** Internet **search tools** and give **one example** each.
answer:
| Search tool | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Search engine** | Uses spiders/robots to collect and index web pages; you query its database. | Google, Bing, Ask |
| **Metasearch engine** | Sends one query to several search engines at once and combines the results. | Dogpile, Yippy, Ixquick |
| **Web (subject) directory/gateway** | Human-organised categories of websites by subject, from broad to narrow. | Yahoo Directory, Lycos |
| **Academic/online database** | Structured collections of scholarly records, often full text. | JSTOR, SAGE, AGORA |

> [!answer]
> Search engines (Google) · metasearch engines (Dogpile) · subject directories (Yahoo) · academic databases (JSTOR).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Search engines** are automated: spiders → index → search interface; huge coverage but variable quality. **Metasearch engines** widen coverage in one query but lose each engine's advanced syntax. **Directories** are human-selected, so quality is better but coverage smaller. **Academic databases** give peer-reviewed, structured, citable records: the best choice for coursework.

## Simplified explanation

**Google** (search engine), **Dogpile** (searches many engines at once), **Yahoo directory** (sites by subject), **JSTOR** (academic articles).
hint: How each tool finds and organises information.

body: Demonstrate with **diagrams** your understanding of the use of the following **Boolean operators** in advanced search: (i) **OR** (ii) **AND** (iii) **NOT**. _(Also asked: mention any two Boolean operators.)_
answer:
Let **A** = `literacy` and **B** = `Ghana`.

**(i) OR: either term (broadens).** `literacy OR Ghana` → everything in A, in B, or in both: **the whole of both circles is shaded**. Use it for **synonyms**: `teenagers OR adolescents`.

**(ii) AND: both terms (narrows).** `literacy AND Ghana` → only records containing **both**: **only the overlap of the circles is shaded**.

**(iii) NOT: exclude a term (narrows).** `literacy NOT Ghana` → records with A but **not** B: **circle A shaded except the overlap with B**.

| Operator | Venn diagram (shaded area) | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **OR** | A ∪ B (both circles) | More results |
| **AND** | A ∩ B (overlap only) | Fewer, more relevant |
| **NOT** | A − B (A without overlap) | Fewer, excludes noise |

> [!answer]
> OR = union (both circles, broadens) · AND = intersection (overlap, narrows) · NOT = A minus B (excludes, narrows).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Boolean logic (George Boole) is the basis of database retrieval. In set notation: OR = $A \cup B$, AND = $A \cap B$, NOT = $A \setminus B$. Many engines treat a space as AND, use `-term` for NOT, and use brackets to nest: `(teenagers OR adolescents) AND smoking`. Use **NOT** carefully: it can drop relevant records that mention both terms.

## Simplified explanation

**AND** = must have both (fewer results). **OR** = either one (more results). **NOT** = leave this out.

> [!tip]
> In the exam, draw **three pairs of overlapping circles** and shade: overlap (AND), everything (OR), left circle minus overlap (NOT).
hint: Draw two overlapping circles for each operator and shade the result.

body: The Internet is a large electronic network which has no centralised control. State and explain **four (4)** criteria you will use to evaluate information taken from the Internet for academic purposes.
answer:
1. **Reliability:** can the source be relied upon? Check the **URL domain**: `.edu` (educational), `.gov` (government), `.org` (non-profit), `.com` (commercial).
2. **Authority:** the basis on which the author speaks: their **recognition in the field, credentials, expertise, educational background, position and institutional affiliation**. Anonymous pages are weak.
3. **Currency/timeliness:** check the **document date**, '**last updated**' date or copyright date, and judge whether it is current enough for the topic.
4. **Accuracy/completeness:** information should be **complete, objective and supported by facts and references**. Consider who provides it and their point of view (bias).
5. **Relevancy:** how well the information **meets your research need** and relates to your topic.
6. **Credibility:** the trustworthiness of the source and its association with credible institutions.

> [!answer]
> Any four, explained: reliability (URL domain) · authority (author's credentials) · currency (dates) · accuracy/objectivity · relevance · credibility.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Because the Internet has **no editorial or central control**, quality control shifts to the reader (ACRL Standard 3). A practical check: read the URL, find the 'About' page and author bio, look for dates and references, cross-check facts in another credible source, and identify the purpose (inform, sell, persuade). Some courses package this as the **CRAAP test** (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose).

## Simplified explanation

Before using a website, ask: **Who wrote it? Is the site trustworthy (.edu, .gov)? Is it recent? Is it accurate? Does it fit my topic?**
hint: Who wrote it, where it comes from, when, how accurate, and how relevant.

body: Explain how the following criteria are used in evaluating information retrieved on the Internet: (i) **Reliability** (ii) **Authority** (iii) **Accuracy**.
answer:
- **Reliability:** examine whether the source can be **relied upon**, chiefly by its **URL**: material from `.edu` (educational institutions), `.gov` (government agencies) and established `.org` sites is generally more reliable than anonymous or commercial (`.com`) pages selling something.
- **Authority:** check **who the author is**: recognition in the field, biographical information, credentials, expertise and educational background, position and institutional affiliation and address. Authority is perhaps the **major criterion**.
- **Accuracy:** check that the information is **correct, complete and objective**, supported by facts, evidence and references, and that you understand the provider's point of view (bias). Cross-check against other credible sources.

> [!answer]
> Reliability: judge the source/URL · Authority: judge the author's credentials · Accuracy: judge the content's correctness and objectivity.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The three work at different levels: **reliability** evaluates the **publisher/domain**, **authority** the **creator**, **accuracy** the **content**. A strong source passes all three; for example, a peer-reviewed article in a university repository (`.edu`) by a named expert with references.

## Simplified explanation

**Reliability** = is the website trustworthy? **Authority** = is the writer an expert? **Accuracy** = are the facts correct?
hint: One criterion is about the site, one about the person, one about the content.

body: Briefly explain the term **bandwidth**.
answer:
**Bandwidth** determines the **speed and amount of data or information transferred** from one place to another on the Internet. It is measured in **bits per second (bps)**, e.g. `kbps`, `Mbps`. **The bigger the bandwidth**, the **greater the volume of information transmitted at a time** and the **faster** information moves.

> [!answer]
> The speed/capacity of data transfer, measured in bits per second; more bandwidth = more data, faster.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bandwidth is the **capacity** of a channel. Dial-up is limited to about `56 kbps`; broadband offers many Mbps. Institutions subscribe to bigger bandwidth so many users can stream, download and use e-resources at once. Remember `1 byte = 8 bits`.

## Simplified explanation

Bandwidth is **how much data your connection can carry per second**: like the width of a pipe.
hint: Definition + unit + effect.

body: Write short notes on **Internet protocol**. _(Also asked: state the standard communication protocols; protocols help computer networks to…)_
answer:
**Internet protocols** are the **set of rules that help the different computer networks on the Internet to communicate without conflict**. The protocols also determine whether a network uses a **peer-to-peer** or **client/server** architecture.

The **standard Internet communication protocols** are **Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)** and **Internet Protocol (IP)**, together **TCP/IP**:
- **TCP** breaks messages into packets and reassembles them reliably at the destination.
- **IP** gives each device an address and routes packets across networks.

_Other protocols:_ HTTP/HTTPS (web), SMTP/POP/IMAP (email), FTP (file transfer).

> [!answer]
> Rules that let different networks communicate without conflict; the standard protocols are TCP and IP (TCP/IP).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Protocols are layered: application protocols (HTTP, SMTP) run over **TCP** (reliable transport), which runs over **IP** (addressing and routing). Because every network speaks TCP/IP, heterogeneous networks interoperate. That is what makes the Internet a 'network of networks'.

## Simplified explanation

Protocols are the **rules computers agree to follow** so they understand each other. The Internet's main ones are **TCP and IP**.
hint: A protocol is an agreed language.

body: (a) What is a **computer network**? (b) Name **four (4)** types of computer networks.
answer:
**(a)** A computer network is a **group of computers connected to each other so that they can share information and electronic resources** (data, hardware such as printers, software). Connections may be by cable, wire, telephone or satellite; a network can have from two to over a million computers. One or more computers act as **host/server** and the others are **clients**.

**(b) Types (by coverage):**
1. **LAN**: Local Area Network: one building or office
2. **CAN**: Campus Area Network: several buildings on one campus
3. **MAN**: Metropolitan Area Network: a city or town
4. **WAN**: Wide Area Network: countries/continents (the Internet is the largest WAN)

> [!answer]
> Connected computers sharing information and resources; LAN, CAN, MAN, WAN.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **server/host** controls access to network resources and provides services to **clients**. Networks may also be classified by architecture (client/server vs peer-to-peer) or topology (star, bus, ring), but ILT 101 classifies them by **geographic span**.

## Simplified explanation

A network is **computers linked to share things**. By size: **LAN** (building) → **CAN** (campus) → **MAN** (city) → **WAN** (world).
hint: Order the types by size.

body: State **two (2)** differences between a **LAN** and a **WAN**.
answer:
| | LAN (Local Area Network) | WAN (Wide Area Network) |
|---|---|---|
| **Coverage** | Small area: a room, building or office | Large area: cities, countries, continents |
| **Speed** | High data-transfer speed | Generally slower (long distances) |
| **Ownership** | Privately owned by one organisation | Often uses leased/public links (telecom, satellite) |
| **Cost/maintenance** | Cheaper, easier to set up | Expensive and complex |
| **Example** | A computer lab | The Internet |

> [!answer]
> Any two: coverage (small vs wide) · speed (fast vs slower) · ownership (private vs leased/public) · cost · example (lab vs Internet).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The key difference is **geographic scope**, which drives the others: short cables give a LAN high speed and low error rates under single ownership; a WAN spans distances using carriers' infrastructure (fibre, satellite, leased lines), raising cost and latency.

## Simplified explanation

A **LAN** is small and fast (one building); a **WAN** is huge (the whole world) and uses telecom links.
hint: Start with geographic coverage.

body: Mention **four (4)** types of **broadband** Internet connections. _(Also asked: mention three types.)_
answer:
1. **Digital Subscriber Line (DSL)** modem connection
2. **Cable modem** connection
3. **Satellite modem** connection
4. **Wireless** connection (Wi-Fi, fixed wireless)
5. **Mobile broadband** (3G/4G/5G)
6. **Fibre-optic** connection

> [!answer]
> DSL · cable modem · satellite modem · wireless · mobile broadband (· fibre).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Broadband** is a generic term for **high-speed, always-on** connections, contrasted with **dial-up** (≤ `56 kbps` over a phone line via a modem that ties up the line). DSL uses telephone lines at higher frequencies; cable uses TV coaxial cable; satellite serves remote areas; mobile broadband dominates in Ghana.

## Simplified explanation

Fast Internet comes through **DSL (phone line), cable, satellite, Wi-Fi or mobile data**.
hint: Broadband = any fast, always-on connection.

body: Give **two (2)** reasons why the **broadband** connection is preferred to **dial-up** connections.
answer:
1. **Higher speed (bandwidth):** broadband offers many Mbps against dial-up's maximum of about `56 kbps`, so pages, downloads and streaming are much faster.
2. **Always-on:** no need to dial up for each session.
3. **Does not tie up the telephone line:** dial-up occupies the phone line; DSL lets voice and data share it.
4. **Supports multimedia and many users**: video conferencing, e-learning, VoIP.

> [!answer]
> Much faster (Mbps vs ≤56 kbps) · always-on · phone line stays free · supports multimedia and multiple users.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Dial-up converts digital signals to analogue via a **modem** over the PSTN, capping throughput at `56 kbps` and occupying the line. Broadband technologies (DSL, cable, fibre, mobile) give far greater **bandwidth** and continuous connections: essential for today's media-rich web and e-resources.

## Simplified explanation

Broadband is **much faster**, **always connected**, and **does not block your phone line**.
hint: Compare speed and convenience.

body: List the types of **databases**. _(Also asked: mention three or four types of databases.)_
answer:
1. **Bibliographic databases**: records with bibliographic details (and abstracts), e.g. indexes
2. **Full-text databases**: the complete text of articles, e.g. JSTOR
3. **Numeric (statistical) databases**: numbers and statistics
4. **Image databases**
5. **Audio databases**
6. **Video databases**
7. **Mixed (multimedia) databases**

> [!answer]
> Bibliographic · full-text · numeric · image · audio · video · mixed.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **database** is a collection of structured records organised for orderly retrieval. Databases are classified by **content**: bibliographic ones point to documents (directional); full-text ones deliver the document itself; numeric, image, audio and video ones store data in those media. Academic databases often combine bibliographic and full-text records.

## Simplified explanation

Databases can hold **references, full articles, numbers, pictures, sound, video, or a mix**.
hint: Classify by what each record contains.

body: Define an **academic database** and give **two (2)** examples. _(Also asked: briefly describe an academic database.)_
answer:
An **academic database** is a **collection of structured records of scholarly literature**, a universal index of periodical literature covering research from all fields of knowledge, with records in **defined fields** (title, author, date, abstract, subject, URL), often with full text, searchable for orderly retrieval.

**Examples:** **JSTOR**, **SAGE Journals**, **AGORA** (agriculture), **Emerald**, **EBSCOhost**, **ScienceDirect**, **Research4Life (HINARI)**.

> [!answer]
> A structured, searchable collection of scholarly records (often full text) with defined fields; e.g. JSTOR, SAGE, AGORA, Emerald.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Unlike the open web, academic databases contain **selected, often peer-reviewed** content, support **field searching, Boolean logic and limits** (date, document type), and give citable records. UCC subscribes to many and makes them available through the library's e-resources portal, including off-campus.

## Simplified explanation

An academic database is an **online collection of research articles** you can search, like **JSTOR**.
hint: Structured · scholarly · searchable · fields.
